sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on chemical-splash goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, and clear the kitchen of children and pets — you will be handling sodium hydroxide and hot soap for the whole session.

Set out a crock pot (or a heavy saucepan you can hold at very low heat, never above 80°C/180°F) plus a stick blender, spatulas, pH strips, and a heat-tolerant soap mold, using only stainless steel, silicone, or heavy plastic — never aluminum.

Weigh every ingredient on a digital scale: 75g cocoa butter, 300g olive oil, 225g rice bran oil (or extra olive oil), 150g coconut oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, and 200g filtered water (use 150g for a harder bar).

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution and the Aloe
steps: In a well-ventilated spot, slowly pour the 100g of sodium hydroxide into the 200g of cool water — always lye into water, never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, keeping your face turned from the fumes.
Set the labeled lye solution aside to cool while you work, out of reach of children and pets.
Blend 50g of fresh aloe vera gel until it is completely smooth and lump-free, and pre-measure your essential oils and French green clay so they are ready the moment they are needed.

sections.title: Melt the Oils & Bring to Trace
steps: Add the cocoa butter, olive oil, rice bran oil, and coconut oil to the crock pot and melt on HIGH for 5-10 minutes, or in the saucepan on very low heat, never letting the oils pass 80°C/180°F.
Blend the French green clay into the melted oils so it disperses without clumps.
Pour the lye solution slowly down the stick blender shaft into the oils and blend in short bursts until the batter starts to emulsify and turn uniformly opaque.
Add the 50g of blended aloe vera gel and keep stick blending until the mixture reaches a very thick trace that holds its shape.

sections.title: Cook to Gel Phase
steps: Cover and cook on low to very low heat for 15-20 minutes; the soap will darken and take on a glossy, vaseline-like translucence as it passes through gel phase — never leave the pot unattended, and stir down the batter with a long whisk if it starts climbing the sides.
Test for full saponification by pressing a pH strip to a smear of cooled batter; it should read below about 10 with no caustic zap remaining.
If any opaque, cream-colored pockets remain in the center, keep cooking in short increments until the whole mass looks translucent.

sections.title: Add Essential Oils, Mold & Unmold
steps: Remove the pot from the heat and let the cooked soap cool for 5-10 minutes so it is no hotter than 80°C/180°F — added hotter, the tea tree and eucalyptus essential oils would simply evaporate.
Stir the essential oils in quickly and thoroughly, as the batter stiffens fast once it starts cooling.

Spoon the thick soap into the mould in stages, banging the mould down on the counter regularly to knock out trapped air pockets, and level the top with a spatula (never bare hands — the soap is still burn-hot).
Allow the soap to cool and harden in the mould for 1-3 days, then remove it and cut it into bars.

tips: Blend the aloe vera gel absolutely smooth before it goes in — intact chunks of aloe can spoil inside the finished bar.

Because saponification finishes in the pot, the tea tree and eucalyptus oils and the aloe keep their character far better than in cold process — but only if you respect the 80°C ceiling when adding them.
Choosing 150g of water instead of 200g gives a harder bar sooner, but the batter will stiffen faster during molding, so work quickly.
homemade-aloe-vera-soap-using-the-hot-pr.cure_and_storage: Let the soap harden in the mould for 1-3 days, cut it into bars, and cure them on wax paper with airflow for 4 weeks before use; store cured bars in a dry, ventilated spot out of sunlight and keep them on a draining dish in the shower.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on protective goggles and gloves plus long sleeves, and keep them on for the entire session — you will handle lye and hot cooked soap.
Set out a slow cooker (large enough that the raw soap fills it no more than half full), a stick blender, digital scale, spatulas, and your soap mold; use no aluminum anywhere.
Weigh the liquid oils — 18 oz olive oil and 1 oz castor oil — directly into the slow cooker.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh 4.9 oz of lye and 11 oz of water separately, replacing some of the water weight with ice cubes to keep the solution cool.
Slowly pour the lye into the water — never water into lye — and stir until fully dissolved, keeping your face away from the fumes in a well-ventilated spot.
Set the labeled lye solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Melt the Fats & Bring to Trace
steps: Weigh and melt the solid fats: 8 oz coconut oil, 6 oz palm oil, and 2 oz shea butter.
Pour the melted fats into the olive and castor oils in the slow cooker and mix well.
Slowly and carefully pour the lye water into the oils while stirring.
Stick blend in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin pudding or gravy consistency — this is trace.

sections.title: The Cook
steps: Set the slow cooker to LOW, put the lid on, and check after 15 minutes; if the batter has separated, simply mix it back together.

Check again in 20-30 minutes — the mixture will begin turning translucent from the hot edges inward, and it may look like apple sauce with a floating glycerin layer; stir that layer back in every 20-30 minutes.

After 1.5-2 hours of cooking and periodic stirring, the whole mass should have a vaseline-like consistency and be neutral (no zap); turn off the slow cooker — and never leave it unattended while it cooks.

sections.title: Add Almond Meal & Mold
steps: Add 5-6 tablespoons of almond meal and 1 tablespoon of intense almond fragrance oil to the cooked soap and mix well.
Working quickly before the batter stiffens, scoop the soap into the mold in stages, banging the mold on the counter after each few scoops to remove air pockets.
Once the loaf is cool and firm, remove it from the mold and cut it into bars — because saponification finished in the pot, the soap can technically be used right away.

tips: Ice cubes counted as part of the 11 oz water weight keep the lye solution cool and shorten the wait before combining.
Stir the almond meal in only after the cook so its gentle scrubby texture survives intact and is evenly suspended in the thick batter.
Note that the intense almond fragrance oil is a synthetic additive — swap it out or reduce it if you want a fully natural bar.
almond-meal-soap.cure_and_storage: The soap is safe to use as soon as it is cool and firm, but the bars will be soft and short-lived; for a harder, longer-lasting bar, cure them on wax paper with good airflow for 4-6 weeks and then store them in a dry, ventilated place out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, clear the room of children and pets, and open a window for ventilation before touching the lye.
Set out a digital scale, stick blender, two non-aluminum pots or pitchers, a thermometer, your mold, and freezer paper and a blanket or towel for covering the poured soap.

sections.title: Make the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh 4.5 oz (128g) of distilled water and 2.14 oz (60g) of food-grade lye into separate containers.
Sprinkle the lye into the water — never the reverse — stirring until fully dissolved, working in a well-ventilated area with your face turned away.
Set the solution aside to cool to around 90-100°F (32-38°C).

sections.title: Weigh & Heat the Oils
steps: Weigh 2.5 oz (71g) of coconut oil (or babassu oil) and melt it gently.
Weigh 12 oz (340g) of olive oil and 1.5 oz (43g) of castor oil into a separate pot.
Pour the melted coconut oil into the olive and castor oils, which brings the combined oils to around 90-100°F.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the warm oils, resting the stick blender shaft against the pot side to prevent splashes.
Mix in alternating short bursts of the stick blender and hand stirring until trace — the batter is thick enough that a drizzle leaves a brief imprint on the surface.
If you want a scented bar, add your essential oils at this stage and stir them in thoroughly.

sections.title: Pour, Insulate & Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold and scrape the pot clean with a spatula.
Cover the surface gently with freezer paper, then wrap the mold with a blanket or towel to hold in the heat of saponification.
After 24 hours remove the cover, and unmold after 2-3 days once the soap is firm — this high-olive recipe stays soft longer than coconut-heavy bars.
Slice the loaf into bars with a sharp knife.

tips: With 75% olive oil this is a gentle, castile-style bar for sensitive skin — expect it to release from the mold slowly and to reward a full, patient cure with real hardness.
The 1.5 oz of castor oil is what gives this simple bar its noticeably better lather — do not skip it.
The recipe is set at a skin-friendly 6% superfat; if you swap any oil, run the change through a lye calculator first.
simple-natural-homemade-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars in open air on wax paper, spaced for airflow, for at least 4 to 6 weeks before use, then store them in a cool, dry, ventilated spot out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Decide your batch size, then run the oil blend — 32% coconut oil, 32% palm oil, 32% olive oil, and 4% castor oil at a 5% superfat — through a lye calculator to get the exact sodium hydroxide and water weights; this recipe deliberately leaves those to your calculator.
Put on goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, clear the room of children and pets, and open a window for ventilation.
Set out a digital scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum lye pitcher and mixing pot, spatulas, and your prepared mold (line a wood mold with freezer paper).

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the calculated distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher set in the sink.
Weigh the calculated lye separately, then slowly sprinkle it into the cool water while stirring — always lye into water, never the reverse — keeping your face turned from the fumes.
Stir until the solution turns clear, then set it somewhere safe to cool to roughly 90-115°F.

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Oils
steps: Weigh and gently melt the coconut oil and palm oil, then stir in the weighed olive oil and castor oil.
Let the combined oils settle to roughly 90-110°F, within about 10-20°F of the lye solution.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Pour
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly down the shaft of the stick blender into the oils to avoid splashes and air bubbles.
Pulse the stick blender in short bursts, hand-stirring in between, until the batter reaches a light trace — uniformly opaque, like thin cake batter that briefly holds a drizzle on its surface.
Pour the batter into the mold in one steady stream, scrape out the pot, and tap the mold firmly on the counter to release air pockets.

sections.title: Insulate & Unmold
steps: Cover the mold and wrap it in a towel if you want a gelled, brighter-colored bar, then leave it undisturbed for 24-48 hours while saponification finishes.
Wearing gloves, unmold once firm and cut the loaf into bars soon after, while it is still easy to slice.

tips: This balanced 32/32/32/4 formula is a classic first recipe — master it plain before adding fragrance or color, since it teaches you exactly what normal trace looks like.
The 4% castor oil is what gives Old Faithful its luscious, stable lather; more than about 5% would make the bar sticky.
Never skip the lye calculator step — the percentages stay the same at any batch size, but the lye and water weights do not.
old-faithful.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars on wax paper with space between them in a dry, dim, airy spot for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally, then store them in a ventilated container out of sunlight; the bar gets milder, harder, and longer-lasting as it cures.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Pick your batch size and run the blend — 25% coconut oil, 25% palm oil, 30% olive oil, 15% sweet almond oil, and 5% mango butter at 5% superfat — through a lye calculator to get your exact lye and water weights.
Suit up in goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, clear the workspace of children and pets, and ventilate the room.
Set out your scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum containers, spatulas, and a lined or silicone mold.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher, then weigh the lye separately.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water while stirring, face turned away from the fumes — never pour water onto lye.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool to roughly 90-115°F.

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil, palm oil, and mango butter gently together — mango butter melts quickly, so keep the heat low.
Stir in the room-temperature olive oil and sweet almond oil, which also helps bring the whole pot down to roughly 90-110°F.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Pour
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils.
Blend in short pulses with hand stirring between bursts until you reach a light trace with no oil streaks.
Pour into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold firmly on the counter to knock out air bubbles.

sections.title: Insulate & Unmold
steps: Cover and towel-wrap the mold if you want gel phase, and leave it undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves on once firm and slice into bars while the loaf is still easy to cut.

tips: The twist here is the 15% sweet almond oil and 5% mango butter, which trade some of Old Faithful's cleansing punch for a noticeably more conditioning, silkier bar.
Mango butter can be swapped for shea butter at the same 5% — but rerun the lye calculator whenever you substitute.
With less coconut and palm than the original, expect a slightly softer loaf; give it the full 48 hours before unmolding.
old-faithful-with-a-twist.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars spaced apart on wax paper in a dry, airy, dim spot for 4-6 weeks, turning them occasionally, then store in a ventilated basket or box away from sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Choose your batch size and run the palm-free blend — 15% coconut oil, 30% canola oil, 25% rice bran oil, 15% shea butter, 10% avocado oil, and 5% chia seed oil at 5% superfat — through a lye calculator for your exact lye and water amounts.
Put on goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, clear the room, and ventilate it before opening the lye.
Lay out your scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum pitcher and pot, spatulas, and mold.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher and the lye into a separate dry container.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water while stirring, keeping your face turned from the fumes — never the reverse order.
Let the labeled solution cool to roughly 90-115°F in a safe spot.

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Oils
steps: Gently melt the coconut oil and shea butter — keep shea on low heat, as overheating can make it grainy.
Stir in the canola, rice bran, avocado, and chia seed oils and bring the mixture to roughly 90-110°F.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Design
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils.
Blend in short pulses with hand stirring between them; with so many slow-moving liquid oils this batter takes its time reaching trace, which is exactly why it suits intricate designs.
Stop at a thin, uniformly opaque trace — this is your window for swirls, layers, or any decorative work you have planned.
Pour into the mold, tap it firmly on the counter, and texture the top if you like.

sections.title: Insulate & Unmold
steps: Cover the mold and leave it undisturbed 24-48 hours; wrap it in a towel only if you want a gelled finish.
Unmold with gloves once firm — the soft-oil-heavy formula may need the full 48 hours or a few hours in the fridge to release cleanly — then cut into bars.

tips: This is a deliberately slow-moving recipe: use the long working time for swirls and intricate designs rather than over-blending it to thick trace.
With only 15% hard coconut oil and no palm, the loaf stays soft longer — be patient before unmolding and give it a full cure.
Chia seed oil is delicate; the 5% superfat helps preserve its skin-conditioning quality in the finished bar.
perfectly-palm-free.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for a minimum of 4-6 weeks on wax paper with good airflow, turning occasionally — soft-oil recipes like this one genuinely need the full cure to harden — then store in a dry, ventilated place away from sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Set your batch size and run the blend — 20% coconut oil, 30% palm oil, 20% canola oil, 4% castor oil, 6% sweet almond oil, 10% rice bran oil, and 10% sunflower oil at 5% superfat — through a lye calculator for exact lye and water weights.
Suit up in goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, ventilate the room, and clear it of children and pets.
Set out your scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum containers, spatulas, mold, and the colorants you plan to swirl, pre-dispersed in a little light oil.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher and the lye into a separate container.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water while stirring, face turned away — always lye into water.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool to roughly 90-115°F.

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Oils
steps: Gently melt the coconut oil and palm oil (fully melt and stir your palm oil container before portioning).
Stir in the canola, castor, sweet almond, rice bran, and sunflower oils and bring everything to roughly 90-110°F.

sections.title: Combine, Color & Swirl
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils and blend in short pulses just to a thin trace — thin batter is essential for clean swirls.
Divide the batter into containers, one per color, and stir your dispersed colorants into each.

Pour the colors back into the mold in alternating passes — down the center, in stripes, or corner to corner — then draw a skewer or chopstick through the batter in loops or figure-eights to create the swirl.
Tap the mold firmly on the counter to settle the batter and release air bubbles, then finish the top with a light swirl of the skewer.

sections.title: Insulate & Unmold
steps: Cover the mold and leave it undisturbed for 24-48 hours; a towel wrap encourages gel phase, which makes swirl colors noticeably brighter.
Unmold with gloves once firm and cut the loaf into bars to reveal the interior swirl pattern.

tips: Work at a thin trace and soap at cooler temperatures — this blend's 46% slow-moving liquid oils were chosen to give you a long window for swirling before the batter thickens.
Fewer skewer passes make bolder swirls; overworking the pattern muddies the colors together.
Gelling the loaf (towel wrap) intensifies swirl colors, but commit fully — a partial gel leaves a visible ring in the bars.
beautiful-swirls.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars on wax paper, spaced for airflow, in a dim dry spot for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally, then store them in a ventilated container out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Set Up the Workspace
steps: Set out all materials on a clean, clutter-free, protected surface: melt and pour soap base, tropical colorants (green, blue, yellow, pink, and orange), coconut or pineapple fragrance oil, a silicone mold, mixing bowls, stirring sticks, and a spray bottle of rubbing alcohol.

Work in a well-ventilated area and wear gloves to avoid skin irritation from concentrated fragrance oils and colorants — no lye is involved in melt and pour, which is what makes this design-focused recipe beginner-safe.
Cut the melt and pour soap base into small, even pieces so it melts quickly and evenly.

sections.title: Melt & Divide the Base
steps: Place the soap base pieces in a microwave-safe container and heat in 30-second intervals, stirring between each, until just fully melted — never let it boil or scorch.
Divide the melted base into separate mixing bowls, one for each tropical color you plan to use.

sections.title: Color & Scent Each Bowl
steps: Add a few drops of a different colorant to each bowl and stir until the color is even, adjusting drop by drop to reach the intensity you want.
Add a few drops of coconut, pineapple, or another tropical fragrance oil to each bowl and stir well to combine.

sections.title: Layer the Colors
steps: Pour the first colored layer into the silicone mold, filling it about one-third full, and lightly spray the surface with rubbing alcohol to pop any bubbles.
Let the first layer cool until it forms a skin, about 10-15 minutes, so the next pour cannot break through it.
Pour the second color on top, spritzing again with rubbing alcohol both to remove bubbles and to weld the layers together.
Continue layering the remaining tropical colors, letting each layer set slightly and spritzing between pours, until the mold is filled.

sections.title: Harden, Unmold & Finish
steps: Let the soap harden fully at room temperature, typically a few hours, before touching the mold.
Carefully flex the mold and remove the soap, then trim any uneven edges with a knife.

tips: Drag a toothpick or skewer gently through the layers before they fully set to create swirls and more intricate tropical patterns.
A transparent soap base makes the greens, blues, and pinks look more vibrant and translucent, like tropical water.
If you want embeds such as small soap shapes or botanicals, place them in the mold before pouring and make sure the melted base covers them completely.
Pour each new layer only after the previous one has skinned over, or the colors will bleed into each other.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.
tropical-paradise.cure_and_storage: There is no cure time — the bars are ready to use as soon as they are cool and hard; wrap them tightly in plastic wrap to prevent glycerin dew and store them in a cool, dry place out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, ventilate the room, and clear it of children and pets before handling lye.

Set out your scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum containers, spatulas, and mold, and pre-disperse the 1 oz of titanium dioxide pigment, 1 oz of cobalt blue mica, and 1 oz of stormy blue mica each in a little lightweight liquid oil so they are clump-free at trace.
Measure the 1.75 oz of Fresh Snow fragrance oil into a glass container and set it aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly and carefully add 4.9 ounces of lye to 10.4 ounces of distilled water — never water into lye — and gently stir until the lye has fully dissolved.
Set the solution aside to cool; if you would like a harder bar that releases faster from the mold, stir 2 teaspoons of sodium lactate (1 teaspoon per pound of oils) into the cooled lye water.

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Oils
steps: Melt and combine 3.5 ounces of avocado oil, 1 ounce of castor oil, 8.8 ounces of coconut oil, 8.8 ounces of olive oil, 8.8 ounces of palm oil (fully melt and stir the entire palm oil container before portioning), and 4.2 ounces of rice bran oil in a large mixing bowl.
Let both the lye water and the oils cool to 130°F or below, ideally within 10 degrees of each other.

sections.title: Combine, Color & Swirl
steps: Add the lye water to the oils and stick blend the mixture to a very thin trace — thin batter is what makes the alpine swirl possible.
Add the 1.75 ounces of Fresh Snow fragrance oil and blend it in briefly.
Divide the batter into three containers and color one white with the dispersed titanium dioxide, one with the cobalt blue mica, and one with the stormy blue mica, whisking each until even.

Pour the colors into the mold in alternating passes, then drag a skewer or spatula through the batter in sweeping S-curves to create the icy alpine swirl, and tap the mold firmly on the counter to release air bubbles.

sections.title: Insulate & Unmold
steps: Cover the mold and leave it undisturbed for 24-48 hours; a towel wrap encourages gel phase, which makes the blues noticeably more vivid.
Wearing gloves, unmold once firm and cut into bars to reveal the swirl.

tips: Stop stick blending at very thin trace — with three colors to mix and pour, a batter that races to medium trace will bury your swirl.
Titanium dioxide and micas disperse far more smoothly pre-mixed in oil than sprinkled in dry, which prevents white streaks and speckles.
The optional 2 teaspoons of sodium lactate makes this soft-swirl loaf noticeably easier to unmold on schedule.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

True sandalwood (Santalum) essential oil is extremely expensive and sustainability-constrained from over-harvesting, so most soapmakers use a sandalwood fragrance oil or a nature-identical blend instead. Sandalwood powder is best treated as a natural tan-to-reddish colorant additive in cold process soap, not as a reliable scent source.

Atlas cedarwood (max 3%, base note) blends especially well with bergamot, juniper, lavender, rose, and rosemary — use it to fix those faster-fading middle and top notes so the finished bar still smells balanced after a full cure.
alpine-swirl-cold-process-soap.cure_and_storage: Leave the loaf in the mold 24-48 hours, cut it into bars, and cure them spaced on wax paper in a dry, airy, dim spot for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally, before use; store cured bars in a ventilated container away from sunlight.

sections.title: Sculpting Tool, Mold & Prep
steps: Cut sturdy cardboard into a T shape whose arms will rest on the mold rails, draw and cut out a carrot silhouette about 2.5 inches long in the center, and wrap the finished tool in clear packaging tape to make it soap-proof.
Line the tall narrow wood loaf mold with freezer paper, shiny side up.
Measure 2 ounces of Avocado Fragrance Oil and 0.6 ounces of 10X Orange Essential Oil into separate small glass containers.

Disperse 1 teaspoon of brown oxide into 1 tablespoon of a light liquid oil, and 1 teaspoon of Nuclear Orange Pigment into another tablespoon of light oil, using a mini mixer to remove clumps; have 2 tablespoons of walnut shells and 2 teaspoons of orange peel powder nearby.

sections.title: Safety & Lye Solution
steps: Suit up with goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, keep kids and pets out of the soaping space, and work in a well-ventilated area.

Slowly and carefully add 5.6 ounces of lye to 13.2 ounces of distilled water and gently stir until fully dissolved and clear, then set aside to cool; optionally add 2.5 teaspoons of sodium lactate to the cooled lye water for a harder, faster-releasing bar.

sections.title: Oils & Batter Split
steps: Melt and combine 2 ounces of carrot seed oil, 1.2 ounces of castor oil, 2.4 ounces of deodorized cocoa butter, 10 ounces of coconut oil, 13.6 ounces of olive oil, and 10.8 ounces of palm oil (fully melt and mix the palm oil container before portioning) in a large bowl.

Once the lye water has cooled to about 130°F, split off 10 ounces of the oil mixture into a separate container and, with safety gear on, pour off 4.7 ounces of the lye solution into another container — these two will later become the orange carrot.

sections.title: Brown Layer & Carving the Carrot
steps: Slowly add the large batch of lye solution to the large batch of oils and stick blend to thin trace, then blend in the 2 ounces of Avocado Fragrance Oil.
Add all the dispersed brown oxide and the 2 tablespoons of walnut shells and whisk thoroughly; give the batter a few stick blender pulses if needed to reach thin-medium trace.
Pour all the brown soap into the lined mold and tap it firmly on the counter to remove bubbles.

Wait roughly 8-10 minutes for the soap to firm, testing the surface with the carrot tool every 3 minutes or so — it must be firm enough to hold a shape but soft enough to scrape smoothly, and it is better to start slightly early than too late.
Insert the cardboard carrot tool and pull it through the mold, lifting out and discarding the scraped soap into a spare mold; keep the tool tracking the same line so the carrot channel stays narrow.
Work down about three-quarters of the mold, then reverse direction and keep passing back and forth until the tool no longer catches soap.

sections.title: Orange Carrot Pour & Finish
steps: Mix the reserved 4.7 ounces of lye solution into the reserved 10 ounces of oils and stick blend to thin trace.
Blend in the 0.6 ounces of 10X Orange Essential Oil, then whisk in 1.5 teaspoons of the dispersed Nuclear Orange Pigment and 2 teaspoons of orange peel powder.

Gently pour the orange soap into the carved channel until it sits level with the brown soap, let any leftover orange batter thicken slightly and pour it down the middle to build a rounded center, then smooth the top with a small spoon.
Cover the mold and leave it undisturbed for 24-48 hours, then unmold with gloves on and cut the loaf into bars to reveal the carrot cross-section in every slice.

tips: The timing of the carve is everything: test the brown soap every 3 minutes and start as soon as it barely holds a shape — once it gets too thick there is no going back.
Keep the carrot tool riding on the mold rails and in the same track on every pass, or the carrot cross-section will come out wide and blurry.
Walnut shells and orange peel powder make this a genuinely scrubby gardener's bar — whisk them in rather than stick blending so they stay evenly suspended.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
carrot-cold-process-soap.cure_and_storage: After 24-48 hours in the mold, unmold, cut into bars, and cure them spaced on wax paper in a dry, dim, airy spot for 4-6 weeks before use; store cured bars in a ventilated container out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, ventilate the room, and clear it of children and pets before opening the lye.
Weigh out all ingredients on a digital scale: 500g olive oil, 500g beef tallow, 300g water, 134.87g sodium hydroxide, and the essential oil blend of 10 ml eucalyptus, 5 ml rosemary, and 5 ml pine.
Set out a stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum lye pitcher and soaping pot, spatulas, and your mold.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly sprinkle the 134.87g of lye into the 300g of cool water while stirring — always lye into water, never the reverse — with your face turned from the fumes.
Stir until the solution is clear, then set it aside, labeled, to cool toward the recipe's working temperature of 40°C (104°F).

sections.title: Prepare & Melt the Fats
steps: Gently melt the 500g of beef tallow in your soaping pot over low heat.
Stir in the 500g of olive oil and let the combined fats settle to about 40°C (104°F), matching the lye solution.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Essential Oils
steps: With both lye solution and fats at about 40°C, pour the lye solution slowly down the stick blender shaft into the fats.
Blend in short pulses, hand-stirring between bursts, until the batter reaches a light trace with no oil streaks.
Stir in the eucalyptus, rosemary, and pine essential oils until fully incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Unmold & Cut
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, scrape the pot clean, and tap the mold firmly on the counter to release air bubbles.
Leave the mold undisturbed and unmold after just 12-18 hours — the tallow-rich formula firms quickly — then cut the loaf into bars while it is still easy to slice.

tips: This traditional olive-and-tallow Marseille-style bar doubles as a household soap: grate 400 grams into 4 litres of water to make laundry gel, and add 1/2 to 1 cup of baking soda to the gel for whites.
The 50% olive oil keeps the bar gentle while the tallow gives early hardness — respect the short 12-18 hour unmold window before the loaf becomes hard to cut.
The piney eucalyptus-rosemary blend fades gently over the cure; store cured bars with a little airflow to keep the scent fresh.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
marseille-soap.cure_and_storage: Unmold after 12-18 hours, cut into bars, and cure them on wax paper with airflow in a dry, dim spot for 4-6 weeks before use; store finished bars in a ventilated container out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Calculate, Safety & Setup
steps: Run the recipe through SoapCalc for your batch size to get the finite amounts of fats, lye, and water: the blend is 55% liquid oils, 20% beef tallow, 20% coconut oil (RBD), and 5% castor oil, plus 10g white kaolin clay, 5g French green clay, and 5g sodium lactate.
Put on your safety gear — gloves and eye protection at minimum, with an apron a good idea — and ventilate the room.
Prepare your mould: a loaf mould works beautifully for the sculpted top, though a cavity mould is fine too.

sections.title: Lye Solution & Oils
steps: Mix up your lye water — always adding lye to the water — using ice for part of the water weight to speed cooling, and let it cool to about room temperature.
Melt the beef tallow, coconut oil, castor oil, and your liquid oils together in the soaping pot and let them cool until just slightly warmer than room temperature.
Stir the 5g of sodium lactate into the cooled lye water, and blend the 10g of white kaolin clay into the melted fats until smooth.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Split
steps: Gently pour the lye mixture into the melted fats and bring the batter to a thin trace with short stick blender pulses.
Pour about 1/4 to 1/3 of the batter into a second container and blend the 5g of French green clay into that portion.

sections.title: Layer, Sculpt & Saponify
steps: Pour the uncoloured kaolin portion into the loaf mould, then knock the mould on the countertop to level it and work out bubbles.
Gently spoon the green clay batter on top of the uncoloured layer, smooth it, and sculpt the top as you like — a spatula mohawk gives it the signature rustic ridge.
Leave the mould undisturbed to saponify for about 36 hours.

sections.title: Unmould & Cut
steps: Once the soap is firm enough to slice (about 36 hours), unmould it; if you used a flexible silicone mould, freeze the loaf first to prevent denting on release.
Trim off any dangly bits and slice the loaf into bars.

tips: Soaping at just-above-room-temperature keeps this batter slow and controllable, which makes the two-layer clay pour easy even for beginners.
Kaolin in the main batter and French green clay on top give slip and a natural two-tone finish without any synthetic colorant.
The 5g of sodium lactate in the lye water hardens the bar for cleaner unmoulding — and freezing a silicone-moulded loaf before release prevents dents.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.
rustic-clay-soap.cure_and_storage: Leave the bars to age and dry for 3-4 weeks before using, spaced on a rack with airflow, then store them in a dry, ventilated spot out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Run your chosen oils through a lye calculator to get exact sodium hydroxide and distilled water weights, then suit up in goggles and gloves and clear a well-ventilated workspace.
Prepare your mold and set out your fragrance oil or essential oil, pigment, and any other optional additives so everything is within reach.

sections.title: Make the Lye Solution
steps: Place a heavy plastic, heat-resistant glass, or stainless steel container on the scale, press tare to zero it, and slowly pour in distilled water to your target weight — be accurate.
Tare a second container and slowly pour in the sodium hydroxide to its target weight, gloves on.
In a well-ventilated area, slowly pour the sodium hydroxide into the water — never pour water into sodium hydroxide — and stir with a spatula until well mixed, avoiding the fumes.
Set the hot solution aside to cool to between 95°F and 105°F.

sections.title: Weigh & Melt the Oils
steps: For each oil or fat in your recipe, tare a container on the scale, weigh the oil to its exact amount, and add it to your stainless steel soap pot.
Melt any solid oils and fats over medium heat, stirring gently and never leaving the pot unattended — you want to gently melt, not overheat.
Turn off the burner and let the oils cool to between 95°F and 105°F, using your thermometer to track both pot and pitcher.
While everything cools, weigh out your fragrance, color, and additives — as a rule of thumb, no more than about 0.6 ounces of fragrance per pound of oils.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: With safety gear back on and mold, oils, lye solution, and additives all at your station, slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring with a whisk, then scrape the sides.

Submerge the stick blender completely and mix in short bursts, working the edges and bottom of the pot and scraping down the sides so no unmixed lye or oil remains (hand stirring also works — it just takes much longer).
Blend until the mixture reaches trace: thin enough to pour off a spoon but thick enough to leave a visible trail on the surface, about like cake batter.
Add your fragrance, color, and any other additives now, whisking or blending until fully incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate & Unmold
steps: Slowly pour the wet soap into the mold, getting it into all the corners, then lightly tap the mold on the work surface to settle it and release trapped air.
Wrap or cover the mold with a heavy blanket or towel and let it rest for 12-24 hours while it heats up and cools down — that warmth is saponification happening.
Once fully cooled, unmold; if the soap is still soft, let it rest 1-3 days more, then cut into bars.

tips: Weigh everything with the tare method described — accuracy with lye and water is what makes a batch safe, and volume measurements are never accurate enough.
Master this basic uncolored, lightly scented process before attempting swirls or milk soaps; fragrance oils can accelerate trace, so add them at a thin trace and be ready to pour.
Keep notes of temperatures, timings, and amounts each batch — the same recipe behaves differently as variables change, and notes turn accidents into lessons.
the-beginner-s-guide-to-making-cp-soap.cure_and_storage: After cutting, set the bars aside in a cool area with good air circulation for 4-6 weeks until fully hard; cured bars store best with space between them in a dry, ventilated, dim spot.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, and long sleeves, ventilate the room, and clear it of children and pets before handling lye.
Brew and completely cool 3/4 cup of chamomile tea — it must be cold before it meets the lye — and measure out 1/4 cup of 100% sodium hydroxide lye.

Make sure your 1 teaspoon each of dried calendula petals, dried chamomile flowers, and dried ground comfrey root or leaves are fully dried — any moist plant material can cause spoilage in the finished soap.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye-Tea Solution
steps: Slowly add the lye to the cold chamomile tea exactly as you would with water — always lye into liquid, never the reverse — stirring until dissolved and keeping your face away from the fumes; the tea will darken and heat up, which is normal.
Set the solution aside until its temperature comes down to about 100°F.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Combine 2/3 cup olive oil, 2/3 cup coconut oil, and 2/3 cup of a vegetable oil blend (such as grapeseed, safflower, and sunflower) in a non-aluminum pot.
Heat just enough to melt the coconut oil, bringing the combined oils to about 100°F to match the lye solution.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add the Botanicals
steps: Slowly mix the lye solution into the oils and stir by hand for 5 minutes.
After 5 minutes, keep stirring or switch to an immersion blender in short bursts until the batter thickens to a pudding-like consistency — this is trace.
At trace, add the dried calendula petals, dried chamomile flowers, and dried ground comfrey, and stir well to distribute them evenly through the batter.

sections.title: Mold & Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into your molds, scraping the pot clean, and tap the molds to release air bubbles.
Remove the soap from the molds after 24 hours and cut it into smaller bars if you used a large mold.

tips: Chamomile tea replaces the water in the lye solution here, layering the herb's soothing character into the very structure of the bar — brew it strong and chill it completely first.
Every botanical must be bone-dry: fresh calendula, chamomile, or comfrey carries water that will spoil the soap from within.
Calendula petals are one of the few flowers that hold their golden color in cold process soap, so save a pinch to sprinkle on top of the poured batter.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
calendula-chamomile-and-comfrey-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars for 3-4 weeks on a rack with good airflow in a dry, dim spot before using, then store them in a ventilated container away from sunlight and humidity.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Gather all ingredients and equipment before you start: 300g organic shea butter, 200g organic olive oil, 150g organic coconut oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, and 20g lavender essential oil, plus a scale, stick blender, thermometer, stainless steel pot, and molds.
Put on protective gear — gloves and goggles at minimum, with long sleeves and good ventilation — and keep children and pets out of the workspace.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Carefully add the 100g of lye to the 220g of distilled water while stirring — always lye into water, never the reverse — with your face turned away from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Melt the Butters & Oils
steps: Melt the shea butter, coconut oil, and olive oil together in a stainless steel pot over gentle heat, keeping the temperature low so the shea butter does not scorch.
Let both the oils and the lye solution come to around 100-110°F (38-43°C) before combining.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Lavender
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils, resting the stick blender shaft against the pot to prevent splashing.
Mix with the stick blender in short bursts until the batter reaches trace — a pudding-like consistency that holds a trail on the surface.
Stir in the 20g of lavender essential oil until fully incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour the mixture into molds and tap them firmly on the counter to remove air bubbles.
Allow the soap to set undisturbed for 24 hours.
Wearing gloves, remove the soap from the molds and cut it into bars.

tips: At 300g, shea butter is nearly half this formula — melt it gently and soap at the stated 100-110°F to avoid graininess in the finished bar.
Add the lavender essential oil at trace, not before, so its relaxing scent survives saponification as fully as possible.
A butter-heavy batter like this can thicken quickly once trace begins, so have your molds ready before you start blending.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-and-shea-butter-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars for 4-6 weeks in a well-ventilated area, spaced apart and turned occasionally, then store them in a cool, dry spot with airflow; the shea-rich bar grows noticeably milder and harder as it cures.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Gather everything before starting: 250g organic coconut oil, 250g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 230g distilled water, 15g rosemary essential oil, and 10g peppermint essential oil, along with scale, stick blender, thermometer, stainless steel pot, and molds.
Put on gloves and goggles with long sleeves, work in a ventilated space, and keep children and pets away.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Carefully add the 100g of lye to the 230g of distilled water while stirring — never pour water onto lye — keeping your face turned from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Gently melt the 250g of coconut oil in a stainless steel pot, then stir in the 250g of olive oil.
Let both the oils and the lye solution come to around 100-110°F (38-43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Essential Oils
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils down the shaft of the stick blender.
Blend in short bursts, hand-stirring between them, until the batter reaches trace and holds a light trail on its surface.
Stir in the 15g of rosemary and 10g of peppermint essential oils until fully incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour the batter into molds and tap them on the counter to release air bubbles.
Let the soap set undisturbed for 24 hours, then unmold with gloves on and cut into bars.

tips: The simple 50/50 coconut-olive base is forgiving and slow-tracing — ideal for getting the invigorating rosemary-peppermint blend mixed in evenly before the batter thickens.
Peppermint reads stronger than rosemary in the cured bar, which is why the recipe uses 15g rosemary to 10g peppermint — resist the urge to even them up.
Coconut oil at 50% makes a hard, bubbly, quite cleansing bar; if your skin runs dry, this is a great invigorating morning or gardener's soap rather than a face bar.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
rosemary-mint-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a well-ventilated area, spaced on wax paper and turned occasionally, then store in a cool, dry place with airflow; the minty sharpness mellows into a clean herbal scent as the bars cure.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on gloves and goggles with long sleeves, ventilate the room, and keep children and pets away while you work with lye.

Weigh out everything first: 200g organic coconut oil, 200g organic olive oil, 150g organic shea butter, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, 30g honey, and 50g rolled oats ground into a fine powder.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly add the 100g of lye to the 220g of distilled water — never water onto lye — stirring until dissolved with your face turned from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the shea butter and coconut oil gently in a stainless steel pot, then stir in the olive oil.
Let both the oils and the lye solution come to around 100-110°F (38-43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Oats and Honey
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils down the stick blender shaft and blend in short bursts until the batter reaches trace.
Stir in the 50g of finely ground oats and 30g of honey until fully incorporated — work the honey in thoroughly so it cannot pool and scorch.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap them on the counter to release air bubbles, and leave them to set for 24 hours.
Do not insulate this batch — honey's sugars make the soap self-heat aggressively, and a wrapped mold can overheat, crack, or volcano.
Wearing gloves, unmold after 24 hours and cut into bars.

tips: Grind the rolled oats to a fine powder — coarse flakes feel scratchy and can go musty in the bar, while oat flour gives the gentle, silky exfoliation this recipe is loved for.
Honey soaps run hot: skip the towel wrap, and if your kitchen is warm consider setting the filled mold somewhere cool.
Warm the 30g of honey slightly before adding so it disperses evenly at trace instead of sinking in ribbons.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
oatmeal-honey-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a ventilated rack, spaced apart and turned occasionally; the honey darkens the soap to a warm gold over the cure, and finished bars keep best in a dry, airy spot away from sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Suit up in gloves, goggles, and long sleeves, ventilate the room, and clear it of children and pets.
Weigh out 250g organic coconut oil, 250g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 230g distilled water, 20g tea tree essential oil, and 10g activated charcoal powder.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly add the lye to the 230g of distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until clear, face turned from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.
Bring both oils and lye solution to around 100-110°F (38-43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Tea Tree and Charcoal
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils and stick blend in short bursts until the batter reaches trace.
Stir in the 20g of tea tree essential oil and the 10g of activated charcoal powder until the batter is an even, streak-free charcoal gray.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour into molds, tap firmly to release air bubbles, and let the soap set for 24 hours.
Unmold with gloves on and cut into bars.

tips: Pre-disperse the activated charcoal in a spoonful of the warm oils before trace to avoid gray clumps and speckles in the finished bar.
Charcoal bars can leave dark lather residue in a light-colored soap dish at first — this fades as the bar cures fully.
Tea tree's medicinal punch softens during the cure, leaving a clean, clinical scent that suits this purifying bar.

Use USED (already-brewed) coffee grounds, patted dry on a towel, as the exfoliant. Dry, unbrewed grounds can bleed and leave a brown halo of color in the bar. A good starting rate is about 1 teaspoon of grounds per pound of soap, added at trace; increase from there for a scrubbier bar. Grounds are a large, aggressive exfoliant, best for feet, elbows, and gardener bars.

Strong brewed coffee can replace part or all of the water in the lye solution, but chill it completely (cold or even frozen) before adding lye. Like milk and teas, a warm sugary liquid plus lye heat leads to scorching and off odors; any odd scent in fresh coffee soap fades during cure.

Activated charcoal dosing (The Nerdy Farm Wife's tested table, per pound of oils): 1/8 to 1/2 tsp gives light-to-medium gray soap with white lather; 1 tsp gives dark gray soap with a faint gray lather; 2 tsp to 1 tablespoon gives black soap but noticeably gray lather that can temporarily mark washcloths and soap dishes. Stay at or below about 1 tsp PPO if white lather matters.

Cocoa powder: about 1 teaspoon per pound of soap at light trace yields a medium chocolate brown (start at 1/2 tsp PPO and work up). Always sift and pre-disperse it in a little light oil or water because it clumps, and choose Dutch-process cocoa for a darker, richer brown than natural cocoa.
tea-tree-and-charcoal-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a ventilated rack, turning occasionally, then store them in a dry, airy place out of sunlight.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on gloves, goggles, and long sleeves, ventilate the workspace, and keep children and pets out.
Weigh out 300g organic coconut oil, 200g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, 30g lemon essential oil, and 20g poppy seeds.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly add the lye to the 220g of distilled water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved with your face turned away.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently, then stir in the olive oil.
Bring both the oils and lye solution to around 100-110°F (38-43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Lemon and Poppy Seeds
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils and stick blend in short bursts to trace.
Stir in the 30g of lemon essential oil and 20g of poppy seeds until evenly distributed.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour into molds and tap them on the counter to knock out air bubbles.
Let the soap set for 24 hours, then unmold with gloves and cut into bars.

tips: Add the poppy seeds at a slightly thickened trace so they stay suspended through the bar instead of sinking to the bottom of the mold.
Citrus essential oils fade faster than most — 30g is a generous dose, and storing the cured bars wrapped or boxed helps the lemon brightness last.
The 20g of poppy seeds gives real scrub; halve them if you want a gentler everyday bar.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
lemon-poppy-seed-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a rack with good airflow, turning occasionally, then store in a cool, dry, ventilated spot away from sunlight to preserve the lemon scent.

sections.title: Safety & Setup
steps: Put on gloves, goggles, and long sleeves, ventilate the room, and keep children and pets away.
Weigh out 250g organic coconut oil, 250g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, 100g coconut milk, and 15g turmeric powder.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Slowly add the lye to the 220g of distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until clear, keeping your face from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.
Bring both oils and lye solution to around 100-110°F (38-43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Coconut Milk and Turmeric

Do not insulate — the milk sugars make this batter run hot, and wrapping the mold risks scorching and cracking.

tips: Because the coconut milk goes in at trace rather than into the lye, it keeps its creaminess — but treat the filled mold like any milk soap and keep it cool rather than insulated.

Weigh out 250g organic coconut oil, 250g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, 20g peppermint essential oil, 15g eucalyptus essential oil, and 10g tea tree essential oil.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Mix the lye slowly into the distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until dissolved.
Allow the labeled solution to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.
Bring both mixtures to around 100-110°F.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add the Essential Oils
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils and stick blend in short bursts until trace.
Stir in the 20g of peppermint, 15g of eucalyptus, and 10g of tea tree essential oils thoroughly.

sections.title: Mold, Set & Cut
steps: Pour into molds and tap out air bubbles.
Let the soap set for 24 hours, then unmold with gloves and cut into bars.

tips: This is the undecorated version of the peppermint-eucalyptus-tea tree bar — same 20/15/10 blend, plain smooth tops, ideal if you plane or stamp your bars.
Pre-mix the three oils so the blend disperses evenly in a single pour at trace.
All three oils are steady at trace, keeping the batter workable throughout.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
peppermint-eucalyptus-tea-tree-soap-vari.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a ventilated rack, turning occasionally, then store them in a cool, dry, airy spot away from sunlight.

Weigh out 300g organic coconut oil, 200g organic olive oil, 100g sodium hydroxide, 220g distilled water, and 20g lavender essential oil, grind 3 tablespoons of oatmeal, and set the dried rose petals aside for decoration.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Mix the lye slowly into the distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until dissolved.
Allow the labeled solution to cool.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.
Bring both mixtures to around 100-110°F.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add Lavender and Oatmeal
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils and stick blend in short bursts until trace.
Stir in the 20g of lavender essential oil and the ground oatmeal thoroughly until evenly suspended.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate & Cut
steps: Pour into molds and tap firmly to release air bubbles.
Press the dried rose petals onto the tops of the soap for decoration.
Let the soap set for 24 hours, then unmold with gloves and cut into bars.

tips: This variation drops the rose essential oil and leans on lavender alone, with a heartier 3 tablespoons of oatmeal for real texture.
Pressing the petals into a slightly thickened surface anchors them better than scattering on liquid batter.
Grind the oatmeal finely for gentle exfoliation that suits sensitive skin.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-rose-petal-oat-soap-variation-2.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a rack with airflow, turning occasionally, then store them in a dry, dim, ventilated spot away from sunlight.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Mix the lye slowly into the distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until dissolved.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils

tips: Lime fades fast in cold process — the sturdy lemongrass carries the citrus theme in the cured bar, with the coconut oil base adding its own creamy note to the tropical profile.

Scatter the dried lemongrass thinly so the tops stay neat when the bars are handled.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
coconut-lemongrass-lime-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on a ventilated rack, turning occasionally, then store them in a cool, dry spot away from sunlight to preserve the lime brightness.

steps: Mix the lye slowly into the distilled water — always lye into water — stirring until dissolved.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.

sections.title: Combine, Trace & Add the Spice Blend
steps: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils and stick blend in short bursts only to a thin trace — cinnamon and clove will accelerate the batter sharply from here.
Stir in the 20g of cinnamon, 15g of patchouli, and 10g of clove essential oils quickly by hand and move straight to the pour.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate & Cut
steps: Pour into molds without delay and tap firmly to release air bubbles.
Dust the ground cinnamon over the tops for decoration.
Let the soap set for 24 hours, then unmold with gloves and cut into bars.

tips: With both cinnamon and clove aboard, this is the fastest-moving batter in the collection — stage the mold at your elbow and stop blending at thin trace.
Cinnamon and clove are strong skin sensitizers; keep to the stated 20g and 10g and consider this a hand or occasional-use bar for sensitive skin.
Dust the cinnamon garnish lightly through a small sieve for an even, bakery-style finish.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. sections.title: Mix the Lye into the Coconut Milk
steps: Weigh 140g of coconut milk into the heat-safe pitcher - use it cold from the refrigerator, since milk sugars scorch if the lye solution gets too hot.

Weigh 70g of sodium hydroxide separately, then add the lye to the coconut milk a little at a time, stirring until fully dissolved - always lye into liquid, never the reverse - with your face turned away from the fumes.
Allow the mixture to cool; a slight yellow or orange tint from the milk sugars is normal.

steps: Melt the 400g coconut oil and 150g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Stir in the 100g olive oil and 50g castor oil off the heat to complete the oil blend.
Let both the lye mixture and the oils cool to around 110°F (43°C).

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Scent
steps: Slowly pour the lye mixture into the oils, stirring continuously.
Use the stick blender in short bursts until the soap reaches trace - thickened to the consistency of thin custard.
Add the 20g coconut fragrance oil and blend thoroughly.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Cut
steps: Pour the soap into your molds in a steady stream.
Sprinkle dried coconut flakes over the top if you want the light exfoliating finish.
Let the soap set in the molds for 24-48 hours, then unmold wearing gloves and cut into bars.

steps: Weigh the 150g of coconut milk cold into the heat-safe pitcher, per the base recipe's lye step.
Weigh 70g of sodium hydroxide separately, then add the lye to the coconut milk a little at a time, stirring until dissolved - always lye into liquid - with your face turned away from the fumes.
Let the mixture cool while you prepare the oils.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 400g coconut oil and 200g palm oil in a double boiler until fully liquid - this variation swaps the original's shea butter for palm, giving a firmer, longer-lasting bar.
Stir in the 100g olive oil and 50g castor oil.

steps: Slowly pour the lye mixture into the oils, stirring continuously.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Cut
steps: Pour the soap into the molds and tap them on the counter to release air.
Let the soap set in the molds for 24-48 hours, then unmold wearing gloves and cut into bars.

tips: Keep the coconut milk icy cold and add the lye in small increments so the milk sugars do not scorch and yellow the pearly-white bars.
Do not insulate the mold - milk soaps overheat easily and a clean white bar depends on staying cool.
White mica shows best against an ungelled, matte batter, another reason to keep this loaf cool while it sets.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

If full-milk lye feels risky, use a split method: dissolve the lye in part water (for example half water, half milk, or a water-discounted lye solution), then blend the reserved milk into the batter at trace. This greatly reduces the chance of scorching.

For a light, creamy-colored bar, avoid gel phase: do not cover or insulate a milk soap, and put the mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours after pouring. Milk's natural sugars make the soap heat up, and gel phase darkens milk soaps.
Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.

steps: Pour the soap into the molds and tap out the air pockets.

tips: Check the batch in a lye calculator and use its water figure for the lye solution - the 150g hibiscus tea is the trace addition, as written.
Hibiscus color shifts dramatically at soap pH - the red mica does the visual heavy lifting, so do not skip it if you want pink bars.
The tea's fruit acids gently exfoliate; this bar suits weekly-glow routines rather than delicate facial skin.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

True sandalwood (Santalum) essential oil is extremely expensive and sustainability-constrained from over-harvesting, so most soapmakers use a sandalwood fragrance oil or a nature-identical blend instead. Sandalwood powder is best treated as a natural tan-to-reddish colorant additive in cold process soap, not as a reliable scent source.

Atlas cedarwood (max 3%, base note) blends especially well with bergamot, juniper, lavender, rose, and rosemary — use it to fix those faster-fading middle and top notes so the finished bar still smells balanced after a full cure.
sandalwood-serenity-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars for 4-6 weeks in a cool, dry, airy place, turning them occasionally. Store cured bars with airflow; the warm, woody scent deepens as the bars age.
