Lavender essential oil is one of the best-behaved oils in cold process and keeps its calming scent through a long cure.
This is a natural bedtime bar - the olive-and-shea base is gentle enough for nightly use.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
rosemary-relaxation-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the cut bars 4-6 weeks in a cool, dry, ventilated spot, turning them occasionally. Store cured bars away from light; the crisp rosemary scent holds well for months.

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

steps: Weigh the 150g of coconut milk cold into the heat-safe pitcher - chilled milk resists scorching when the lye heats it.

Weigh 70g of sodium hydroxide separately, then add the lye to the coconut milk a little at a time, stirring until dissolved - always lye into liquid, never the reverse - with your face turned away from the fumes.
Let the mixture cool; a warm cream tint from the milk sugars is normal.

Stir in the 100g olive oil and 50g sweet almond oil.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Cut
steps: Pour the soap into the molds and tap them on the counter to release air.
Let the soap set in the molds for 24-48 hours, then unmold wearing gloves and cut into bars.

tips: Vanilla naturally darkens soap toward caramel-brown during the cure - lean into it; it suits this dessert-like bar.
Keep the coconut milk icy and the mold uninsulated so the milk sugars neither scorch nor overheat.
The shea-almond-coconut combination makes one of the creamiest, most moisturizing bars in the collection.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

If full-milk lye feels risky, use a split method: dissolve the lye in part water (for example half water, half milk, or a water-discounted lye solution), then blend the reserved milk into the batter at trace. This greatly reduces the chance of scorching.

For a light, creamy-colored bar, avoid gel phase: do not cover or insulate a milk soap, and put the mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours after pouring. Milk's natural sugars make the soap heat up, and gel phase darkens milk soaps.
Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.

tips: Cinnamon essential oil is a strong accelerant and skin irritant in excess - respect the 20g measure, add at thin trace, and pour fast.

A light hand with the ground cinnamon keeps the bar swirled rather than scratchy.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Cinnamon and clove essential oils are potent skin sensitizers with small safe caps: keep cinnamon leaf EO to about 0.5% of soap weight or less (roughly 40 drops per pound of soap; cinnamon bark is even more restricted, about 0.2%), and Soap Queen's blending guide caps clove leaf EO at 1.44 oz per 48 oz of cold process soap. Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

Eugenol-rich spice oils (clove, cinnamon leaf) react with lye and accelerate trace. Soap at cool temperatures, add the spice EO at thin trace, use the stick blender only in ~3-second bursts (or hand-whisk to emulsion), and have your mold prepped before pouring.

steps: Melt the 400g coconut oil, 200g palm oil, 100g olive oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Let the oils cool to around 110°F (43°C), close to the lye solution's temperature.
Pre-measure the 20g honeysuckle fragrance oil and set out the dried hibiscus petals.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Honeysuckle
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Blend in short pulses until a thin cake-batter trace forms, usually 2-10 minutes.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, tap out air bubbles, and smooth the top.
Sprinkle dried hibiscus petals over the surface for decoration.
Cover and insulate with a towel for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves on and cut into bars.

tips: Floral fragrance oils like honeysuckle can accelerate trace — have your mold ready and add the fragrance at a thin trace so you have time to pour.
Hibiscus tea's ruby color usually shifts toward muted mauve or gray in high-pH soap; use the dried petals on top for reliable color.
Dissolve the lye in most of the hibiscus tea (the recipe's only liquid) and hold back only a splash for trace.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh 150g of the cold coconut milk into the pitcher, reserving a spoonful to blend in at trace as the original recipe adds milk at that stage.

Sprinkle the 70g sodium hydroxide into the cold coconut milk a little at a time, stirring constantly — always lye into liquid, never liquid onto lye — and pause between additions so the milk does not overheat and turn orange.
Stir until fully dissolved, then let the labeled solution cool to around 110°F (43°C) or below.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 400g coconut oil, 200g palm oil, 100g olive oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C), within 10-20°F of the lye solution.
Pre-measure the 20g coconut fragrance oil and set out the shredded coconut.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Coconut
steps: Pour the lye-milk solution slowly down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Pulse in short bursts, hand-stirring in between, until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace (2-10 minutes).
Blend in the reserved coconut milk and the 20g coconut fragrance oil, then stir in shredded coconut if you want a gently exfoliating bar.

sections.title: Mold and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the molds, tap them on the counter to release air, and smooth the tops.
Do not insulate — coconut milk's sugars make this batter prone to overheating, so leave the mold uncovered in a cool spot (or refrigerate it) for 24-48 hours.
Wearing gloves, unmold the firm soap and cut it into bars.

tips: Always add lye to cold or slushy coconut milk in small increments; hot lye scorches milk sugars and discolors the soap.
Skip the towel insulation on this recipe — milk soaps overheat easily and can crack or volcano in the mold.
Shredded coconut makes a noticeable scrub; toast-dry, finely shredded coconut gives the smoothest feel.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

If full-milk lye feels risky, use a split method: dissolve the lye in part water (for example half water, half milk, or a water-discounted lye solution), then blend the reserved milk into the batter at trace. This greatly reduces the chance of scorching.

For a light, creamy-colored bar, avoid gel phase: do not cover or insulate a milk soap, and put the mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours after pouring. Milk's natural sugars make the soap heat up, and gel phase darkens milk soaps.
Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.
coconut-paradise-soap.cure_and_storage: After the 24-48 hours in the mold, cut the loaf and air-cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a cool, dry, ventilated place as the recipe directs, then store them with airflow away from humidity.

tips: Vanilla naturally discolors cold process soap toward caramel and deep brown over the cure — embrace the warm tone rather than fighting it.
True vanilla essential oil is rare; if you substitute a vanilla fragrance oil, check that it is soap-safe and expect stronger browning.
The vanilla tea is the recipe's only liquid, so dissolve the lye in it and hold back just a splash for trace.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Cinnamon and clove essential oils are potent skin sensitizers with small safe caps: keep cinnamon leaf EO to about 0.5% of soap weight or less (roughly 40 drops per pound of soap; cinnamon bark is even more restricted, about 0.2%), and Soap Queen's blending guide caps clove leaf EO at 1.44 oz per 48 oz of cold process soap. Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on chemical-splash goggles, nitrile gloves, long sleeves, an apron, and closed-toe shoes, and clear the kitchen of children, pets, and distractions.

Work near an open window and set out a digital scale, stick blender, thermometer, a heat-safe non-aluminum pitcher for the lye, a stainless steel pot for the oils, silicone spatulas, and your mold — aluminum reacts dangerously with lye and must not touch any part of this recipe.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh 150g of distilled water into the lye pitcher.

Weigh 70g of sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container, then slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water while stirring — always lye into water, never water onto lye — keeping your face turned away from the fumes.
Stir until every granule dissolves, then set the labeled solution in a safe, ventilated spot to cool to around 110°F (43°C), about 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Weigh the 500g olive oil, 200g coconut oil, and 100g palm oil into your pot and melt them in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C) so oils and lye solution are within 10-20°F of each other.
Pre-measure the 20g rosemary essential oil and 10g lemon essential oil, and set out the dried rosemary leaves.

steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly down the shaft of the stick blender into the oils, stirring continuously.

Pulse the blender in short bursts, hand-stirring between them, until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace with no oil streaks — with 500g of olive oil this can take a little longer than average.
Blend in the 20g rosemary essential oil and 10g lemon essential oil until evenly incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the molds, tap them on the counter to release air bubbles, and smooth the tops.
Sprinkle dried rosemary leaves over the surface for a Mediterranean finish.
Cover and insulate with a towel, leaving the mold undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Wearing gloves, unmold the soap and cut it into bars — olive-heavy loaves may need an extra day or two before they release cleanly.

tips: At 62% olive oil this bar leans castile-style: slow to trace, slow to harden, and wonderfully mild after a long cure.
Lemon essential oil fades fast in cold process soap; the rosemary will carry most of the finished scent.
Run the 70g lye figure through a lye calculator against these exact oils before starting, as with any published recipe.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.

Dissolve the lye in most of the argan tea and hold back only a splash for trace, since the tea is the recipe's only liquid.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

tips: Matcha gives a lovely natural green that softens toward sage over time — keep the cured bars out of sunlight to slow the fading.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Cool the oils to roughly 110°F (43°C), close to the lye solution's temperature.
Pre-measure the 20g vanilla essential oil and set aside a vanilla bean for decorating the top.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Vanilla
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Pulse in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace, usually 2-10 minutes.
Blend in the reserved vanilla tea and the 20g vanilla essential oil until evenly incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, tap out air pockets, and smooth the top.
Press a split vanilla bean gently onto the surface for decoration if you like.
Cover and insulate with a towel for 24-48 hours.
Wearing gloves, unmold and cut into bars.

tips: Vanilla reliably browns cold process soap over the cure — this bar is meant to wear warm caramel tones, and the cocoa butter suits that character.
True vanilla essential oil is scarce; if you use a vanilla fragrance oil instead, confirm it is skin-safe for soap and expect deeper browning.
Dissolve the lye in most of the vanilla tea (the recipe's only liquid) and hold back only a splash for trace.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Cinnamon and clove essential oils are potent skin sensitizers with small safe caps: keep cinnamon leaf EO to about 0.5% of soap weight or less (roughly 40 drops per pound of soap; cinnamon bark is even more restricted, about 0.2%), and Soap Queen's blending guide caps clove leaf EO at 1.44 oz per 48 oz of cold process soap. Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

Eugenol-rich spice oils (clove, cinnamon leaf) react with lye and accelerate trace. Soap at cool temperatures, add the spice EO at thin trace, use the stick blender only in ~3-second bursts (or hand-whisk to emulsion), and have your mold prepped before pouring.
tahitian-vanilla-bean-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, dim, ventilated place, turning them occasionally; the color deepens as they age, and cured bars store best with open airflow.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Wear goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes for the whole session, and keep children and pets away.

Ventilate the workspace and set out your scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum lye pitcher, stainless steel pot, spatulas, and individual cavity molds if you have them — salt bars harden too fast to slice cleanly from a loaf.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: The published recipe says to mix the lye with water but does not state the amount, so run the formula through a lye calculator for 70g sodium hydroxide with these oils and weigh out that distilled water.
Slowly sprinkle the 70g sodium hydroxide into the cool water while stirring — always lye into water, never water onto lye — with your face turned away from the fumes.
Stir until dissolved and let the labeled solution cool to about 110°F (43°C), roughly 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 400g olive oil, 200g coconut oil, 100g palm oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C), within 10-20°F of the lye solution.
Pre-measure the 150g fine Maldivian sea salt and the 20g sea breeze fragrance oil, and pre-disperse a pinch of blue mica in a spoonful of oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Sea Salt
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Pulse in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace, usually 2-10 minutes.
Blend in the 20g sea breeze fragrance oil and the dispersed blue mica, then stir in the 150g sea salt by hand — the batter will thicken quickly once the salt goes in.

sections.title: Mold and Unmold Early
steps: Pour or spoon the thick batter into the molds immediately, pressing it in and smoothing the tops.

Leave the molds in a cool spot and check every few hours: salt bars set rock-hard fast, so unmold (and cut, if using a loaf) as soon as the soap is firm — often within 4-12 hours, well before the usual 24-48.
Wear gloves for all handling; the soap is still caustic while it finishes saponifying.

tips: Use fine-grain sea salt — coarse crystals make a scratchy bar and can cause crumbling at the edges.
Cut or unmold salt soap early; wait a full day and the loaf will shatter rather than slice.
Salt mutes lather, so the high coconut-and-salt combination is intentional here — expect a dense, lotion-like lather and a spa-hard bar.

Formulate salt bars with 50-100% of the oil weight in fine-grain sea salt (beginners start at 50%) and a coconut-oil-heavy base with a high superfat, because salt suppresses lather; Soap Queen's salt bar runs 50% coconut oil and many formulas go 80-100% coconut with 15-20% superfat.

Cut salt bars EARLY, in hours not days: salt makes the batter harden extremely fast, so a loaf must be unmolded and cut as soon as it is firm, roughly 1-6 hours after pouring depending on the recipe. Wait overnight and the loaf crumbles when cut. Individual cavity molds sidestep the timing problem entirely.

Use plain fine sea salt or Himalayan pink salt, not Dead Sea salt or Epsom salt. Dead Sea salt's very high mineral content is strongly hygroscopic, pulling moisture from the air and producing weepy, sweaty, soft bars.

Add fruit or vegetable purees at thin trace. Sugary purees (strawberry, banana, mango) speed up trace and heat the soap, so soap at cooler temperatures, skip insulation, and refrigerate or freeze the mold after pouring, since overheated sugar can crack, volcano, or caramelize the bar to a dull brown.
maldivian-sea-salt-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the salt bars for 4-6 weeks in a dry, ventilated place — they only get milder and harder with age — and store them away from humidity, which salt readily attracts.

steps: The recipe says to mix the lye with water without stating an amount, so run the formula through a lye calculator for 70g sodium hydroxide with these oils and weigh out that distilled water — the split-liquid method (lye in water, milk at trace) is a classic way to keep milk from scorching.

steps: Melt the 400g olive oil, 200g coconut oil, 100g palm oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C), within 10-20°F of the lye solution.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Coconut Milk
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.

sections.title: Mold and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, tap out air bubbles, and smooth the top.
Sprinkle shredded coconut over the surface for decoration.
Do not insulate — milk sugars overheat easily; leave the mold uncovered in a cool spot (or refrigerate) for 24-48 hours.
Wearing gloves, unmold the soap and cut it into bars.

tips: Adding the coconut milk at trace (the split method) keeps its sugars away from raw lye heat and preserves a creamy white bar.
Because the milk adds extra liquid at trace, the loaf may stay soft an extra day — be patient before unmolding.
The recipe omits the lye water amount; a lye calculator fills that gap — never guess.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

If full-milk lye feels risky, use a split method: dissolve the lye in part water (for example half water, half milk, or a water-discounted lye solution), then blend the reserved milk into the batter at trace. This greatly reduces the chance of scorching.

For a light, creamy-colored bar, avoid gel phase: do not cover or insulate a milk soap, and put the mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours after pouring. Milk's natural sugars make the soap heat up, and gel phase darkens milk soaps.
Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.
seychellois-coconut-milk-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, dim, ventilated spot, turning them occasionally, then store the finished soap with open airflow away from humidity.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Cinnamon and clove essential oils are potent skin sensitizers with small safe caps: keep cinnamon leaf EO to about 0.5% of soap weight or less (roughly 40 drops per pound of soap; cinnamon bark is even more restricted, about 0.2%), and Soap Queen's blending guide caps clove leaf EO at 1.44 oz per 48 oz of cold process soap. Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

Eugenol-rich spice oils (clove, cinnamon leaf) react with lye and accelerate trace. Soap at cool temperatures, add the spice EO at thin trace, use the stick blender only in ~3-second bursts (or hand-whisk to emulsion), and have your mold prepped before pouring.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

steps: In a separate pitcher, sprinkle the 70g sodium hydroxide into the 150g cold coconut milk a little at a time, stirring constantly and pausing between additions — always lye into liquid, never the reverse.

steps: Pour the lye-milk solution slowly down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.

sections.title: Mold and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, tap out air bubbles, and smooth the top.
Do not insulate — coconut milk overheats easily; leave the mold uncovered in a cool spot (or refrigerate) for 24-48 hours.
Wearing gloves, unmold the fast-hardening soap and cut it into bars — check at 24 hours, as high-coconut loaves get harder to slice the longer they sit.

tips: Castor oil at 50g is the lather booster here, teaming with the 400g coconut oil for big fluffy bubbles.
High-coconut bars can feel drying on some skin; the coconut milk fat offsets it, but cut and cure promptly and test after curing.
Add lye to icy coconut milk in increments — scorched milk means an orange, sour-smelling bar.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.

steps: Pour the batter into the mold, tap out air bubbles, and smooth the top.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.

steps: Put on chemical-splash goggles, nitrile gloves, long sleeves, an apron, and closed-toe shoes, and clear the kitchen of children, pets, and distractions.

Filter the seawater well (a coffee filter works) and let it cool to room temperature — clean seawater makes this a natural brine (soleseife) soap.

sections.title: Prepare the Seawater Lye Solution
steps: Weigh 150g of the filtered, cooled seawater into the pitcher, reserving a spoonful for the trace addition in the original instructions.
Slowly sprinkle 70g sodium hydroxide into the cool seawater while stirring — always lye into liquid, never the reverse — keeping your face away from the fumes.
Stir until dissolved and let the labeled solution cool to about 110°F (43°C), roughly 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 400g olive oil, 200g coconut oil, 100g palm oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C), within 10-20°F of the lye solution.
Pre-measure the 20g ocean breeze fragrance oil and pre-disperse a pinch of blue mica in a spoonful of oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Ocean Breeze
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Pulse in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace — brine batters can firm faster than plain water ones, so watch closely.
Blend in the reserved seawater and the 20g ocean breeze fragrance oil, then add the dispersed blue mica and mix until the sea-glass blue is even.

sections.title: Mold and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold promptly, tap out air bubbles, and smooth or wave-texture the top.
Cover lightly and leave the mold in a cool spot for 24-48 hours, checking early — the salt content firms the loaf quickly.
Wearing gloves, unmold the soap and cut it into bars as soon as it is firm enough to slice cleanly.

tips: Seawater's dissolved salts make a harder, stone-smooth bar with a dense, lotion-like lather — the soleseife tradition this recipe echoes.
Cut brine soap on the early side; left too long it becomes brittle and crumbles under the knife.
Dissolve the lye in most of the seawater (the recipe's only liquid) and hold back just a splash for trace.
ocean-breeze-escape.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a dry, ventilated place, turning them occasionally, and store cured bars away from humidity — salt bars readily pull moisture from damp air.

Weeks ahead, steep sandalwood chips in a carrier oil such as olive oil, then strain — have 150g of this sandalwood-infused oil ready at room temperature.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: The sandalwood infusion is an oil and cannot dissolve lye, and the published recipe lists no water — run the formula through a lye calculator for 70g sodium hydroxide with these oils and weigh out that distilled water.
Slowly sprinkle the 70g sodium hydroxide into the cool water while stirring — always lye into water, never water onto lye — with your face turned away from the fumes.
Stir until dissolved and let the labeled solution cool to about 110°F (43°C), roughly 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 400g olive oil, 200g coconut oil, 100g palm oil, and 50g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid.
Cool the oils to around 110°F (43°C), within 10-20°F of the lye solution.
Pre-measure the 20g sandalwood fragrance oil and pre-disperse pinches of red and yellow mica in separate spoonfuls of oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Sandalwood
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils, stirring continuously.
Pulse in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin cake-batter trace, usually 2-10 minutes.
Blend in the 150g sandalwood-infused oil and the 20g sandalwood fragrance oil — the infusion acts as a woody superfat — then swirl in the red and yellow micas for a sunset-wood effect.

sections.title: Mold, Unmold and Cut
steps: Pour the batter into the molds, tap out air pockets, and smooth or swirl the tops.
Cover lightly and leave the mold undisturbed for the recipe's 24-48 hours, then unmold wearing gloves.
Cut the loaf into bars while it slices cleanly.

tips: Adding 150g of infused oil at trace raises the superfat substantially — expect a rich but softer bar, allow extra mold time, and verify the full formula in a lye calculator.

The recipe lists no lye water; a lye calculator supplies it — never guess.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

Sandalwood powder is best treated as a natural tan-to-reddish colorant additive in cold process soap, not as a reliable scent source.

sandalwood-serenade.cure_and_storage: After unmolding at 24-48 hours, cure the bars for the additional 4-6 weeks the recipe calls for, in a well-ventilated, dry, dim spot, and store cured bars with open airflow.

Swirl the bowl gently so the two oils marry.

steps: Add the 2 tablespoons of distilled water to the essential oil mixture and stir well.
Pour the mixture into the spray bottle, using the funnel if needed.
Screw on the atomizer top firmly and label the bottle with its contents and the date.

sections.title: Gather Supplies
steps: Set out 10 drops of grapefruit essential oil, 8 drops of lemongrass essential oil, 2 tablespoons of jojoba oil, and a clean rollerball bottle.
Check that the rollerball and cap are clean, dry, and seat firmly.
Work over a wipeable surface with a small funnel or steady pour.

sections.title: Blend the Essential Oils
steps: Add the 10 drops of grapefruit essential oil and 8 drops of lemongrass essential oil directly into the rollerball bottle.
Count drops carefully; the 10-to-8 ratio balances sparkling citrus against the grassy-lemon depth.

sections.title: Add the Carrier and Seal
steps: Add the 2 tablespoons of jojoba oil to the essential oil mixture and mix well.
Secure the rollerball top onto the bottle and screw on the cap.
Roll the bottle between your palms for several seconds to finish blending, then label it with the name and date.

sections.title: Apply and Enjoy
steps: Patch test on your inner forearm before regular use.
Roll the blend onto pulse points, such as wrists and neck, for a refreshing and uplifting aroma.
Because grapefruit is a citrus oil that can react with sunlight, apply to skin that stays covered if you will be outdoors, and reapply as the scent softens.

tips: Citrus oils like grapefruit can be phototoxic; avoid direct sun on freshly applied skin for 12 hours.
Jojoba is technically a liquid wax that mirrors skin sebum, making it a long-lasting, non-greasy carrier.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

Any fragrance containing vanillin will discolor cold process soap from off-white to dark brown over days to weeks — the higher the vanillin percentage, the darker the final bar. Oxidation from light and air drives it, so browning spreads fast once bars are cut. Either choose a vanillin-free fragrance for pale designs or plan the palette around the brown (coffee, chocolate, spice-latte looks).

Vanilla color stabilizer is only reliable in melt-and-pour soap, used at a 1:1 ratio with the fragrance oil. In cold process its results are inconsistent — it may merely delay browning by a few months — so Soap Queen advises not to rely on it for CP; titanium dioxide can lighten only low-vanillin (tan) discoloration.

Cinnamon and clove essential oils are potent skin sensitizers with small safe caps: keep cinnamon leaf EO to about 0.5% of soap weight or less (roughly 40 drops per pound of soap; cinnamon bark is even more restricted, about 0.2%), and Soap Queen's blending guide caps clove leaf EO at 1.44 oz per 48 oz of cold process soap. Treat these as hard maximums, not targets.

Eugenol-rich spice oils (clove, cinnamon leaf) react with lye and accelerate trace. Soap at cool temperatures, add the spice EO at thin trace, use the stick blender only in ~3-second bursts (or hand-whisk to emulsion), and have your mold prepped before pouring.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on chemical-splash goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes before touching the lye, and keep them on for the entire session.

Work in a well-ventilated room with no children or pets nearby, and set out your digital scale, stick blender, thermometer, heat-safe non-aluminum lye pitcher, mixing pot, spatulas, and soap mold before you start.

Weigh every ingredient rather than measuring by volume: 800 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 200 g shea butter, 140 g sodium hydroxide, and 340 ml distilled water, and confirm the amounts in a lye calculator as a final check.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 340 ml of distilled water into the heat-safe pitcher and the 140 g of sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water — never pour water onto lye — stirring gently with a heat-proof spoon until every granule dissolves, keeping your face turned away from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution in a safe, ventilated spot and let it cool toward the 40-50°C working range, which typically takes 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt the Olive Oil, Coconut Oil and Shea Butter
steps: While the lye cools, melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler until fully liquid, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.

Bring the combined oils to roughly 40-50°C so the oils and the lye solution are within about 10 degrees of each other; if you plan to scent the bars, pre-measure your optional essential oil blend now.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: With safety gear still on, slowly pour the cooled lye solution into the oils, guiding it down the shaft of the stick blender to prevent splashes and air bubbles.

Blend in short bursts, hand-stirring between pulses, until the batter reaches trace — uniformly opaque and thickened like thin custard, leaving a brief trail on the surface; this usually takes 2-10 minutes.
If using the optional essential oil blend, add it at light trace and mix thoroughly until no oil streaks remain.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into your mold in one steady stream, scraping the pot with a spatula, then tap the mold firmly on the counter to release air pockets.
Cover the mold with cardboard or a lid and wrap it with a towel to insulate, leaving it undisturbed for 24-48 hours while saponification completes.
Wearing gloves, unmold the soap once firm and cut the loaf into bars with a sharp knife or wire cutter while it is still easy to slice.

tips: With 800 g of olive oil this is a high-olive, castile-style bar; it may need an extra day or two in the mold before it is firm enough to unmold cleanly.
Soap with the lye and oils at moderate, closely matched temperatures for a slow-moving, beginner-friendly batter.
Master this plain base batch before adding fragrance; it teaches you exactly how the batter behaves at trace.
olive-oil-delight-soap.cure_and_storage: Stand the cut bars on parchment with space between them in a dry, airy spot out of direct sunlight and cure for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. The high olive oil content means the bars keep hardening and improving for months; store finished soap in a cool, dry place with airflow rather than sealed plastic.

Work in a ventilated area free of children and pets, with scale, stick blender, thermometer, non-aluminum lye pitcher, oil pot, and mold set out.

Weigh 800 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 200 g shea butter, 140 g sodium hydroxide, and 340 ml distilled water, plus the pomegranate seed oil and pomegranate fragrance oil, and check the recipe in a lye calculator.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 340 ml distilled water into a heat-safe pitcher and the 140 g lye into a dry container.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, face away from the fumes.
Cool the labeled solution toward 40-50°C, roughly 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt the Olive Oil, Coconut Oil and Shea Butter
steps: Melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.
Bring the oils to about 40-50°C and pre-measure the pomegranate seed oil and pomegranate fragrance oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Pomegranate Duo
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils down the blender shaft.
Blend in short bursts with hand-stirring between, stopping at a light thin-custard trace.
At light trace, add the antioxidant-rich pomegranate seed oil and the pomegranate fragrance oil and hand-stir thoroughly until evenly blended.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold on the counter to release air pockets.
Cover with cardboard and a towel and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves once firm and cut into bars while still easy to slice.

tips: Adding the pomegranate seed oil at trace preserves it as a superfatting oil so more of its vitamins survive saponification.
Fruity fragrance oils can accelerate trace; stay at light trace, stir by hand, and check the supplier's IFRA rate before scaling up.
Some berry-type fragrance oils discolor soap; test a small batch with your specific pomegranate fragrance first.
pomegranate-pleasure-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, ventilated spot out of the sun, turning the bars occasionally. Store in a cool, dry, airy place; the sweet fruity scent typically holds well for a year.

Weigh 800 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 200 g shea butter, 140 g sodium hydroxide, and 340 ml distilled water, plus the fennel and orange essential oils, and verify the recipe in a lye calculator.

Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved with your face turned away.

steps: Melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.
Bring the oils to roughly 40-50°C and pre-blend the fennel and orange essential oils in one container.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add Fennel and Orange
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils down the stick blender shaft.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold to knock out air bubbles.

tips: Sweet fennel's licorice-like anise note is strong and long-lasting; let the orange play the brighter supporting role in the blend.
Fennel essential oil should be used sparingly and is best avoided by pregnant users; keep the usage rate low and note the oil on your label.
The orange top note fades in the cure while fennel persists, so the balance will shift toward licorice over time.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
fennel-fusion-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, airy spot away from sunlight, turning the bars occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place with airflow; expect the anise note to outlast the citrus.

tips: Cypress and pine oils oxidize as they age, which dulls the fresh evergreen scent; use recently purchased oils for the best result.
Conifer oils behave well at trace, keeping this an easy, slow-moving batter for beginners.
An optional pinch of green clay or nettle powder dispersed in oil would echo the forest theme without changing the recipe's structure.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

True sandalwood (Santalum) essential oil is extremely expensive and sustainability-constrained from over-harvesting, so most soapmakers use a sandalwood fragrance oil or a nature-identical blend instead. Sandalwood powder is best treated as a natural tan-to-reddish colorant additive in cold process soap, not as a reliable scent source.

Atlas cedarwood (max 3%, base note) blends especially well with bergamot, juniper, lavender, rose, and rosemary — use it to fix those faster-fading middle and top notes so the finished bar still smells balanced after a full cure.
cypress-forest-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, ventilated spot out of the sun, turning the bars occasionally. Store in a cool, dry, airy place; the woodsy evergreen scent mellows gracefully over several months.

steps: Melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Basil
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils down the stick blender shaft.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold to knock out air bubbles.

tips: Sweet basil essential oil is intense and green; a modest usage rate gives a fresh herb-garden bar without overwhelming the nose.
Choose the linalool chemotype of basil oil for a softer, more floral-leaning scent that suits the Blossom name.
Basil holds its scent through the cure better than citrus, so no fixative is needed.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
basil-blossom-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, airy spot away from sunlight, turning the bars occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place with airflow; the herbaceous scent stays clean and fresh for many months.

Weigh 800 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 200 g shea butter, 140 g sodium hydroxide, and 340 ml distilled water, plus the honey and fig fragrance oils and the finely diced dried figs, and check the recipe in a lye calculator.

sections.title: Prepare the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 340 ml distilled water into a heat-safe pitcher and the 140 g lye into a dry container.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved with your face turned away.
Cool the labeled solution toward 40-50°C, about 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt the Olive Oil, Coconut Oil and Shea Butter
steps: Melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.
Bring the oils to roughly 40-50°C; dice the dried figs finely and pre-blend the honey and fig fragrance oils.

sections.title: Bring to Trace, Scent, and Fold in the Figs
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils down the stick blender shaft.
Blend in short bursts, hand-stirring between, until the batter reaches a light thin-custard trace.
At light trace, add the honey and fig fragrance oils and stir well, then fold the finely diced dried figs into the batter just before pouring for texture and visual appeal.

sections.title: Mold, Keep It Cool, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold to knock out air bubbles.
Cover only lightly — the fig pieces and honey-type fragrance carry natural sugars that make the loaf run warm — and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves once firm and cut into bars while the loaf slices easily.

tips: Dice the dried figs very small; large sticky chunks can spoil, drag at cutting, and fall out of the finished bar.
Sugary inclusions push the batch toward overheating, so insulate lightly and watch for a center crack.
Both fragrance oils should be checked against their IFRA certificates, and sweet gourmand fragrances often darken the soap slightly.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
honey-fig-fusion-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure for 4-6 weeks on parchment in a dry, airy spot away from sunlight, turning the bars occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place with airflow and use within a year, since the fruit inclusions make this bar happiest used fresh.

steps: Melt the 200 g coconut oil and 200 g shea butter in a double boiler, then stir in the 800 g olive oil.

sections.title: Bring to Trace, Color and Scent
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils down the stick blender shaft.
Blend in short bursts with hand-stirring between until the batter reaches a thin-custard trace.

sections.title: Mold, Salt the Top, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, scrape the pot, and tap the mold on the counter to release air bubbles.
Once the surface has set up slightly, sprinkle sea salt across the top for decoration and texture.
Cover loosely, leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours, then unmold wearing gloves and cut into bars while the loaf slices easily.

tips: Disperse the mica in oil before adding to avoid streaks and speckles in the blue-green color.
Sprinkle the sea salt only after the surface firms slightly so the crystals perch on top instead of sinking.
Cut the loaf on its side so the salt crown does not drag through the bar faces, and check the fragrance oil's IFRA rate.

Formulate salt bars with 50-100% of the oil weight in fine-grain sea salt (beginners start at 50%) and a coconut-oil-heavy base with a high superfat, because salt suppresses lather; Soap Queen's salt bar runs 50% coconut oil and many formulas go 80-100% coconut with 15-20% superfat.

Cut salt bars EARLY, in hours not days: salt makes the batter harden extremely fast, so a loaf must be unmolded and cut as soon as it is firm, roughly 1-6 hours after pouring depending on the recipe. Wait overnight and the loaf crumbles when cut. Individual cavity molds sidestep the timing problem entirely.

Use plain fine sea salt or Himalayan pink salt, not Dead Sea salt or Epsom salt. Dead Sea salt's very high mineral content is strongly hygroscopic, pulling moisture from the air and producing weepy, sweaty, soft bars.

Add fruit or vegetable purees at thin trace. Sugary purees (strawberry, banana, mango) speed up trace and heat the soap, so soap at cooler temperatures, skip insulation, and refrigerate or freeze the mold after pouring, since overheated sugar can crack, volcano, or caramelize the bar to a dull brown.

tips: Keep the lavender buds on top only; buds mixed into the batter turn brown and look like specks of dirt.
Lemon fades faster than lavender in the cure, so the lemonade note is brightest in the first months.
Both oils are well behaved at trace, keeping this a relaxed, beginner-friendly pour.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, add a face mask for the lye stage, and wear long sleeves and closed-toe shoes.
Prepare your mold — line a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper — cover the work area with newspaper, and check that all equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the three ingredients exactly: 835 g olive oil, 215 g distilled water, and 107 g lye (sodium hydroxide).

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 215 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container set in the sink, and the 107 g of lye into a separate dry container.

Slowly add the lye to the water — never the other way around — stirring gently until completely dissolved; the solution can exceed 93°C and gives off irritating fumes, so keep your face away and work with strong ventilation.
Set the solution aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); once mixed and cooling, you may remove the face mask.

sections.title: Prepare the Olive Oil
steps: Weigh the 835 g of olive oil into your mixing container.
Warm the oil gently in 30-second microwave bursts or over low heat until it sits in the same 38-43°C range as the lye solution, or simply let the lye cool down to match the oil's temperature.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: When both liquids are between roughly 32-40°C and close in temperature, slowly pour the lye solution into the olive oil while stirring continuously.

Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts, alternating with hand-stirring, until the batter reaches trace: no free oil floats on top and drips leave a faint trail on the surface — pure olive oil batters can take noticeably longer than blended-oil recipes.
If you wish to scent the bars, stir in your essential oils now until no unincorporated oil is visible.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap it gently on the counter to release air bubbles.
Cover the mold with a lid or cardboard, wrap it in a towel, and leave it undisturbed for 48-56 hours — castile soap needs longer than most before unmolding.
Test by peeling a corner of the liner; when the sides come away cleanly, unmold, and once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Pure olive oil soap is slow to trace and slow to harden; patience at every stage — blending, unmolding, curing — is the whole secret.
If the soap sticks to the liner when you peek, simply wait another 24 hours before trying again.
This single-oil castile bar is the classic gentle soap for sensitive skin; keep the first batch unscented to learn its behavior.
olive-oil-soap.cure_and_storage: Stand the bars on a drying rack in a well-ventilated area for at least 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally — castile genuinely improves for months and is at its best after an extended cure. Store cured bars in a cool, dry place.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, with a face mask ready for the lye stage, and cover your work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper, and check all equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the ingredients: 418 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 167 g palm oil, 42 g castor oil, 17 g honey, 235 g distilled water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 235 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container.
Wearing the face mask, slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring gently until dissolved; the mix heats past 93°C and fumes, so keep your face away and ventilate well.
Set the solution aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Honey
steps: Weigh the 418 g olive oil into a container, adding the 42 g castor oil last since it is heavy and clings to containers.
Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 167 g palm oil in a double boiler or in 30-second microwave bursts until they reach the same 38-43°C range, then combine all oils in the mixing jug.
Warm the 17 g of honey with an equal amount of hot water to thin it, then mix it thoroughly into the warm oils so it distributes evenly.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Optional Scent
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with hand-stirring until the batter reaches trace, with no free oils floating and a faint trail when dripped.
If adding essential or fragrance oils, hand-stir them in now without accelerating trace.

sections.title: Mold, Refrigerate, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently on the counter to release air bubbles.

Cover the mold loosely with plastic film or parchment and place it in the refrigerator for 8-12 hours — chilling stops the honey's sugars from overheating the loaf — then leave it out, undisturbed, another 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold the soap; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or cutter.

tips: Refrigerating instead of insulating is the key honey-soap trick: sugars make the loaf run hot, and chilling prevents cracking, caverns, and scorched color.
Thin the honey with warm water before adding so it disperses instead of pooling into sticky pockets.
Expect a warm tan bar with boosted lather; honey naturally darkens soap.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
honey-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally for even drying. Store the cured bars in a cool, dry place; the emollient honey bar grows milder and harder with time.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, keep a face mask handy for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper, and confirm your equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 412 g olive oil, 206 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41 g castor oil, 233 g distilled water, 116 g lye, your chosen strength of eucalyptus essential oil (up to 24 g for a strong scent), 2 tablespoons white kaolin clay, and your green colorant (1 tablespoon French green clay or spirulina powder, or 1 teaspoon green mica).

sections.title: Blend the Eucalyptus Oil with Clay and Colorant
steps: In a clean glass container, weigh out the eucalyptus essential oil at your chosen scent strength.
Add the 2 tablespoons of white kaolin clay and your green colorant, mix thoroughly, and set aside so the ingredients merge — the clay anchors the fragrance and prevents color speckles.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 233 g of chilled distilled water (or water ice cubes) into a heat-resistant container and the 116 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Wearing the mask, slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, face turned from the fumes, then set aside to cool to 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 206 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil in a double boiler or microwave bursts to the same 38-43°C range; weigh the 412 g olive oil with the 41 g castor oil added last, then combine all oils in the mixing jug and whisk.

Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter just reaches trace — this can take as little as 30 seconds, so go carefully.
Add the eucalyptus-clay-colorant mixture and hand-stir well until no unincorporated oil is visible and the color is uniform.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles; once the surface sets up slightly, sprinkle dry crushed eucalyptus leaves in a line down the middle or one side for decoration.
Cover loosely with plastic film or parchment, wrap with a towel, and leave undisturbed for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Blending the essential oil into kaolin clay before trace anchors the scent and spreads the green color evenly with no speckles.
Stop stick blending at the first sign of trace; this recipe can reach trace in under a minute.
A restrained line of crushed eucalyptus leaves looks better than covering the whole top, and cut bars on their side so leaves do not drag.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.
eucalyptus-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the refreshing balsamic eucalyptus scent is robust and long-lived.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, keep a face mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper, and check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 418 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 167 g palm oil, 41.8 g castor oil, 2 teaspoons granulated sugar, 25 g lavender essential oil, 235 g distilled water, 117 g lye, 2 tablespoons white kaolin clay, and purple clay (1 tablespoon) or purple mica (1 teaspoon).

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 235 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container, then carefully add the 117 g of lye while stirring gently, never the reverse.
Work ventilated with your face away from the fumes, then set the solution aside to cool to 38-43°C (100-110°F); the mask can come off once it is mixed.

sections.title: Blend the Lavender Oil with the Clays
steps: In a glass or stainless container, combine the 2 tablespoons of white kaolin clay, the purple clay or mica, and the 25 g of lavender essential oil.
Blend thoroughly into a smooth paste, adding a splash of olive oil if needed — this anchors the fragrance and prevents color speckles.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 167 g palm oil in 30-second microwave bursts or a double boiler; weigh the 418 g olive oil and 41.8 g castor oil (castor last) into the big mixing container, add the melted oils, and stir in 1-2 teaspoons of sugar for better lather.

When oils and lye are both in the 38-43°C range, slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend in 5-second bursts, stirring well between, until the batter reaches a pancake-batter trace.
Add the lavender-clay mixture and hand-stir well to blend the color evenly; if desired, also stir in a tablespoon of finely ground dried lavender buds for gentle exfoliation.

sections.title: Mold, Texture the Top, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the prepared mold and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Let the surface set to a toothpaste consistency, then texture it with a fork or spoon and sprinkle a light line of whole dried lavender buds down the center.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed 24-48 hours; unmold when the liner peels cleanly and cut into bars once firm.

tips: The teaspoon or two of sugar dissolved in the oils boosts the lather of this palm-and-olive base.
Blending the lavender essential oil into kaolin and purple clay anchors the scent through the cure and gives an even pastel color.
A restrained line of lavender buds on top is prettier than full coverage, and buds stay on the surface where they will not brown.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; lavender is one of the most persistent natural scents and will still be calming months later.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, use a mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold and confirm equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the ingredients: 418 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 42 g castor oil, 42 g avocado oil, 10 g cane sugar, 232 g water, and 115 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 232 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container and the 115 g of lye separately.
Carefully add the lye to the water while stirring gently — never the reverse — in a well-ventilated spot with your face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); never rewarm a cooled lye solution in the microwave, only in a hot water bath.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Sugar
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter gently in a double boiler or 30-second microwave bursts, avoiding scorching the butter.
Weigh the 418 g olive oil and 42 g avocado oil into a separate container, adding the 42 g castor oil last, then combine everything in the mixing jug with 1-2 teaspoons of the sugar.
Stick blend briefly to unify the oils, then check that oils and lye are both in range and within about 10 degrees of each other.

sections.title: Combine, Trace and Optional Additions
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Use the immersion blender in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, thickening slightly and leaving a visible trail when dripped.
If desired, add essential or fragrance oils (ideally blended into a little clay) and stir gently to distribute without accelerating trace.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold and tap gently on the counter to release air bubbles.
