Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Melt the shea butter gently and only until liquid; overheated shea can go grainy in the finished bar.
The avocado oil and 5 percent-style castor addition make this an especially conditioning, label-worthy moisturizing bar.
The cane sugar compensates for the lather-softening effect of the rich butters.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
shea-butter-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally for even drying. Store in a cool, dry place; the shea-rich bar becomes noticeably creamier and milder with a full cure.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask up for the lye stage, and cover your work area.
Prepare the mold in advance and have it right beside your mixing station — this batter sets fast.
Weigh the ingredients: 165 g olive oil, 165 g cocoa butter, 165 g mango butter, 165 g shea butter, 124 g coconut oil, 41 g castor oil, 314 g water, and 110 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 314 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container and the 110 g of lye separately.
Carefully add the lye to the water while stirring gently — never the reverse — ventilated and with your face turned away; remove the mask once fully combined.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Melt the Three Butters and Oils
steps: Gently melt the 124 g coconut oil with the 165 g each of cocoa butter, mango butter, and shea butter in a double boiler or 30-second microwave bursts, taking care not to scorch these delicate butters.
Weigh the 165 g olive oil and 41 g castor oil (castor last) in a separate container, then combine all oils and butters in the mixing jug.

sections.title: Combine and Watch for Fast Trace
steps: Be prepared for this high-butter mixture to move quickly, with the mold ready to go.
Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils, stirring with a whisk or spatula to combine before any stick blending.
Use only short 5-second blender bursts until the batter reaches trace, then stop; if using essential oils, stir them in gently by hand now.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold without delay — the hard butters make it set up very quickly — and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars promptly, as high-butter loaves become hard and crumbly to cut if left too long.

tips: Cocoa, mango, and shea together make the batter race to trace; whisk by hand first and treat the stick blender as a finishing tool.
Cut the bars within a day or so of unmolding — fully hardened triple-butter soap can crack under the knife.
The generous 314 g of water in this recipe deliberately slows the fast-moving butters; do not discount it.
triple-butter-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the exotic butter trio yields a hard, creamy-lathered bar that keeps beautifully.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, with a face mask for both the lye stage and the fine charcoal powder, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper.

Weigh the ingredients: 418 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 167 g palm oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 28 g tea tree essential oil, 10 g lavender essential oil, 2 teaspoons activated charcoal, 235 g water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 235 g of chilled or semi-frozen distilled water into a heat-safe container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated and face turned away, then set aside to cool to 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Make the Charcoal and Essential Oil Paste
steps: Keep your mask on while handling the feather-light activated charcoal until it is fully dampened.
Combine the 28 g tea tree essential oil, 10 g lavender essential oil, and 2 teaspoons of activated charcoal, and mix into a smooth paste; set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 167 g palm oil to the same 38-43°C range; weigh the 418 g olive oil with the 42 g castor oil last, combine everything in the mixing jug with the sugar, and stick blend briefly to unify.
Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter just reaches trace.
Add the tea tree, lavender, and charcoal paste and hand-stir until the black color is completely even with no unincorporated oil.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover loosely with plastic film or parchment and wrap with a towel to support gel phase, leaving it undisturbed for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Wetting the charcoal into an essential oil paste first is the difference between an even slate-black bar and a speckled gray one — and it keeps the dust out of your lungs.
Two teaspoons of charcoal colors the bar without leaving gray marks on washcloths; more is not better.
Tea tree and lavender both hold their scent well, making this a dependable purifying bar for oily skin.

Use USED (already-brewed) coffee grounds, patted dry on a towel, as the exfoliant. Dry, unbrewed grounds can bleed and leave a brown halo of color in the bar. A good starting rate is about 1 teaspoon of grounds per pound of soap, added at trace; increase from there for a scrubbier bar. Grounds are a large, aggressive exfoliant, best for feet, elbows, and gardener bars.

Strong brewed coffee can replace part or all of the water in the lye solution, but chill it completely (cold or even frozen) before adding lye. Like milk and teas, a warm sugary liquid plus lye heat leads to scorching and off odors; any odd scent in fresh coffee soap fades during cure.

Activated charcoal dosing (The Nerdy Farm Wife's tested table, per pound of oils): 1/8 to 1/2 tsp gives light-to-medium gray soap with white lather; 1 tsp gives dark gray soap with a faint gray lather; 2 tsp to 1 tablespoon gives black soap but noticeably gray lather that can temporarily mark washcloths and soap dishes. Stay at or below about 1 tsp PPO if white lather matters.

Cocoa powder: about 1 teaspoon per pound of soap at light trace yields a medium chocolate brown (start at 1/2 tsp PPO and work up). Always sift and pre-disperse it in a little light oil or water because it clumps, and choose Dutch-process cocoa for a darker, richer brown than natural cocoa.
activated-charcoal-and-tea-tree-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place away from light-colored linens, since fresh charcoal bars can transfer a little color at first.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g cocoa butter, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 28 g Vanilla 10X essential oil, 1.5 tablespoons cocoa powder, 1.5 tablespoons rhassoul clay, 237 g water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the chilled or semi-frozen distilled water into a heat-safe container and the sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, well ventilated with your face turned away, then set aside to cool to 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Blend the Vanilla, Cocoa and Rhassoul Clay
steps: Combine the 28 g of Vanilla 10X essential oil, 1.5 tablespoons of rhassoul clay, and the unsweetened cocoa powder in a glass container.
Blend until completely smooth and set aside — this paste is what gives the bar its even chocolate color and warm scent.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, and 125 g unrefined cocoa butter gently to the 38-43°C range; weigh the 334 g olive oil with the 42 g castor oil added last, then combine all oils in the mixing jug.

Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring — this butter-rich batter thickens quickly, so stop at the first slight trace.
Add the cocoa, vanilla, and rhassoul clay mixture and hand-stir gently until evenly blended; the clay and cocoa will thicken the batter further, so work steadily.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the thick batter into the lined mold, tap it firmly on the counter to remove air pockets, and smooth the top with a spatula.
Cover loosely with plastic film or parchment and wrap with a towel, leaving it undisturbed for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Cocoa butter plus cocoa powder plus clay makes one of the fastest-thickening batters in this book; have the mold ready and stop blending early.
Use unsweetened cocoa powder only — drinking-chocolate mixes contain milk solids and sugar that scorch.
Vanilla naturally browns soap, so the bar will deepen toward dark chocolate as it cures; that is part of its charm.

Use USED (already-brewed) coffee grounds, patted dry on a towel, as the exfoliant. Dry, unbrewed grounds can bleed and leave a brown halo of color in the bar. A good starting rate is about 1 teaspoon of grounds per pound of soap, added at trace; increase from there for a scrubbier bar. Grounds are a large, aggressive exfoliant, best for feet, elbows, and gardener bars.

Strong brewed coffee can replace part or all of the water in the lye solution, but chill it completely (cold or even frozen) before adding lye. Like milk and teas, a warm sugary liquid plus lye heat leads to scorching and off odors; any odd scent in fresh coffee soap fades during cure.

Activated charcoal dosing (The Nerdy Farm Wife's tested table, per pound of oils): 1/8 to 1/2 tsp gives light-to-medium gray soap with white lather; 1 tsp gives dark gray soap with a faint gray lather; 2 tsp to 1 tablespoon gives black soap but noticeably gray lather that can temporarily mark washcloths and soap dishes. Stay at or below about 1 tsp PPO if white lather matters.

Cocoa powder: about 1 teaspoon per pound of soap at light trace yields a medium chocolate brown (start at 1/2 tsp PPO and work up). Always sift and pre-disperse it in a little light oil or water because it clumps, and choose Dutch-process cocoa for a darker, richer brown than natural cocoa.
chocolate-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the antioxidant-rich chocolate bar darkens and smells warmer as it matures.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 28 g Orange 10X essential oil, 14 g Lemon 5X essential oil, 14 g grapefruit essential oil, 1.5 tablespoons kaolin clay, 1.5 tablespoons yellow Brazilian clay, 1 teaspoon benzoin powder (optional), 1 tablespoon citrus zest, 237 g water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the chilled or semi-frozen distilled water into a heat-safe container and the sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated with your face turned away, then set aside to cool to 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Make the Citrus Zest, Clay and Benzoin Mixture
steps: Combine the tablespoon of zest with the 28 g Orange 10X, 14 g Lemon 5X, and 14 g grapefruit essential oils in a glass container.
Add the 1.5 tablespoons each of kaolin clay and yellow Brazilian clay plus the teaspoon of benzoin powder, and blend until smooth; the mixture may be thick — set it aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter to the 38-43°C range; weigh the 334 g olive oil, 125 g avocado oil, and 42 g castor oil (castor last), combine everything with the sugar in the mixing jug, and stick blend briefly.
Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter reaches a light trace.
Add the citrus-clay-benzoin mixture and hand-stir until evenly blended; citrus oils tend to slow trace, so a few extra blender bursts may be needed.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles; once it sets up slightly, sculpt the top lightly and sprinkle dried citrus zest for decoration.
Cover loosely with plastic film, cardboard, or parchment and wrap with a towel to insulate for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: The folded Orange 10X and Lemon 5X oils are the secret to citrus that survives the cure; standard-fold citrus would fade to almost nothing.
Benzoin powder acts as a natural fixative, further anchoring the sunny scent.
Prepare citrus zest properly — fully dried, no pith — before it goes anywhere near cold process soap.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
citrus-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place and enjoy within a year, while the refreshing triple-citrus scent is at its energizing best.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, with a face mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area with newspaper.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper, and confirm equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 42 g grapefruit essential oil, 1.5 tablespoons pink clay, 1.5 tablespoons yellow Brazilian clay, 1 tablespoon white kaolin clay, 1 teaspoon benzoin powder (optional), 1 tablespoon grapefruit zest, 237 g water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 237 g of chilled or semi-frozen distilled water into a heat-safe container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the other way around — stirring gently until dissolved, working ventilated with your face turned away from the fumes.
Set the solution aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); the mask can come off now.

sections.title: Make the Grapefruit Zest and Clay Mixture
steps: Combine the tablespoon of grapefruit zest and the 42 g of grapefruit essential oil in a glass container.
Add the pink clay, white kaolin clay, yellow Brazilian clay, and benzoin powder and blend until smooth, thinning with up to a tablespoon of avocado oil if the paste is too thick; set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Weigh the 334 g olive oil, 125 g avocado oil, and 42 g castor oil (castor last) into one container, and melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter to the same 38-43°C range as the lye.
Combine all the oils in the mixing jug, then slowly pour in the lye solution while stirring continuously.

Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with hand-stirring until the batter reaches trace, then add the grapefruit-clay-benzoin mixture and hand-stir until evenly blended — citrus oils may slow trace, so extra blending is fine.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently on the counter to release air bubbles.
Cover loosely with plastic film, cardboard, or parchment and wrap with a towel, leaving it undisturbed for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: The pink and yellow clays give a natural sunrise tone and anchor the fleeting grapefruit scent; benzoin fixes it further.
Grapefruit essential oil fades quickly in cold process; the generous 42 g here plus the fixative is what keeps the finished bar zesty.
Use fully dried grapefruit zest with no pith for flecks that stay golden instead of browning.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
grapefruit-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally for even drying. Store in a cool, dry place and use within a year while the refreshing grapefruit scent is at its peak.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold and check all equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 150 g shea butter, 100 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 30 g tea tree essential oil, 50 g French green clay (or 25 g green plus 25 g white kaolin for a two-color swirl), 228 g distilled water, and 114 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 228 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container.
Carefully add the 114 g of lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until completely dissolved.
Set aside to cool to the cooler-than-usual range of 29-32°C (85-90°F) this recipe uses.

sections.title: Hydrate the Tea Tree and Clay Mixture
steps: In a glass or stainless container, mix the 30 g of tea tree essential oil with the 50 g of French green clay until thoroughly combined, adding a tablespoon of distilled water if too thick.
For a two-color soap, divide the essential oil evenly and mix green clay into one half and white kaolin clay into the other; set aside to hydrate.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 150 g shea butter to the same 29-32°C range; weigh the 334 g olive oil, 100 g avocado oil, and castor oil last into a separate container, then combine everything in the mixing jug and stick blend briefly.
Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend to a thin trace only — the clay mixture will thicken the batter further.
Hand-whisk in the clay and essential oil mixture until the color is completely uniform; for two colors, split the batter roughly in half first and mix one clay blend into each.

sections.title: Mold, Swirl, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold; for a two-color soap, pour the first color, tap flat, add the second, then draw a spoon or chopstick gently through to marble without blending the colors away.
Tap the mold on the counter to bring up air bubbles, decorate the top as desired, cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed 18-24 hours.
When the liner or mold pulls away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Stop at thin trace before the clay goes in; clay drinks up water and can turn the batter to paste if you blend too far first.
The cooler 29-32°C soaping temperature keeps this batter slow enough for the two-color swirl.
French green clay plus tea tree makes this a purifying bar for oily skin — a great one to label as a facial soap.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.
green-clay-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; clay bars appreciate good airflow, as trapped moisture can make their surface sticky.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold and check the equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 417 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 118 g shea butter, 59 g kokum butter, 42 g castor oil, 8 g honey, 30 g chamomile essential oil, 15 g colloidal (finely ground) oats, 13 g rolled oats, 25 g kaolin clay, 234 g distilled water, and 115 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Oat-Infused Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 234 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container and stir in the 15 g of colloidal oats.
Carefully add the 115 g of lye to the oat water — never the reverse — stirring until the lye fully dissolves; the fine oats infuse the solution rather than dissolving.
Set aside to cool to the cooler 29-32°C (85-90°F) range this recipe uses.

sections.title: Blend the Chamomile Oil and Clay, and Prepare the Oils
steps: Mix the 30 g of chamomile essential oil with 25 g of white kaolin clay until smooth, adding a tablespoon of distilled water if too thick, and set aside to hydrate.

Gently warm the 200 g coconut oil, 118 g shea butter, 59 g kokum butter, and the honey together to the same 29-32°C range; weigh the 417 g olive oil with the 42 g castor oil last in a separate container.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the 13 g of rolled oats, and stick blend briefly to distribute them.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Chamomile Clay
steps: Slowly pour the oat-infused lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend to a thin trace only, remembering the oatmeal itself slightly thickens the batter.
Hand-whisk in the chamomile-clay mixture until the batter is one uniform color.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold and tap it on the table to smooth the top and raise air bubbles.
Let the batter firm slightly, sculpt the top, and decorate one side with a mix of dried chamomile flowers and rolled oats.
Cover and insulate for 18-24 hours; when the liner peels cleanly, unmold, and cut the loaf on its side so the blade does not drag the oats through the bar faces.

tips: Colloidal oats in the lye water plus rolled oats in the oils gives both silky skin-soothing and gentle scrub in one bar.
The honey is tiny but still sugar — the cooler soaping temperature keeps the loaf from overheating.
Cutting the loaf on its side prevents the knife catching oats and flowers and gouging the faces.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
oatmeal-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; this gentle exfoliating bar suits sensitive skin best after a full cure.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare the mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 28 g Orange 10X essential oil, 1.5 tablespoons yellow Brazilian clay, 1 tablespoon orange zest, 237 g water, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 237 g of chilled or semi-frozen distilled water into a heat-safe container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated with your face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Make the Orange Zest and Clay Mixture
steps: Combine the tablespoon of orange zest and the 28 g of Orange 10X essential oil in a glass container.
Add the 1.5 tablespoons of yellow Brazilian clay and blend until smooth; the mixture may be thick — set it aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter to the 38-43°C range; weigh the 334 g olive oil, 125 g avocado oil, and 42 g castor oil (castor last), then combine all oils with the sugar in the mixing jug and stick blend briefly.
Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring with a spatula or whisk.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until trace, then hand-stir in the orange-clay mixture until evenly blended — orange oil can slow trace, so extra blending may be needed.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles; once it sets slightly, sculpt the top lightly and sprinkle dried orange zest for decoration.
Cover loosely with plastic film, cardboard, or parchment and wrap with a towel for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: The 10x folded orange oil is what makes this festive scent last; regular orange essential oil would fade during the cure.
Yellow Brazilian clay both colors the bar a warm sunrise shade and helps anchor the citrus.
The cane sugar boosts lather in this shea-and-avocado enriched base.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
orange-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; enjoy within a year while the warm festive orange is strongest.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area — turmeric stains, so protect surfaces well.
Prepare your mold and confirm equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 12 g turmeric powder, 233 g distilled water, 116 g lye, and the 33 g essential oil blend of 23 g eucalyptus, 5 g peppermint, 3 g tea tree, and 2 g spearmint.

sections.title: Mix the Turmeric Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 233 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container.
Carefully weigh the 116 g of lye, add the 12 g of turmeric powder to the mix, and stir the lye and turmeric into the water until combined — the turmeric infuses the solution with its golden color.
Set aside to cool toward the 32-43°C (90-110°F) working range.

sections.title: Blend the Essential Oils and Prepare the Oils
steps: In a glass or stainless container, blend the essential oils: 23 g eucalyptus, 5 g peppermint, 3 g tea tree, and 2 g spearmint, for 33 g total.
Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the sugar and the essential oil blend, and stick blend briefly, checking that oils and lye are both 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the golden turmeric lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Use the immersion blender in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, thickening slightly and leaving a visible trail on the surface.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover the mold with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold once firm — allowing another day or two if still soft — and cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Infusing the turmeric directly in the lye solution gives an even gold-to-amber bar with no speckles.
Turmeric stains fabric and counters, so glove up and protect everything; the finished cured bar, however, will not stain skin.
Adding the essential oils to the oils before the lye, as this recipe does, is unusual but works here because the eucalyptus-mint blend is trace-stable.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
turmeric-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place away from direct light, which can fade turmeric's golden color over time.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold and confirm equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the ingredients: 619 g olive oil, 165 g coconut oil, 41 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 25 g vanilla essential oil (3 percent of oils), 227 g distilled water, and 113 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: With your mask on and without leaning over the container, weigh the 227 g of distilled water into a heat-resistant container.
Carefully weigh the 113 g of lye, add it to the water, and stir until dissolved.
Set aside to cool; remove the mask once the solution is fully mixed.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Vanilla
steps: Weigh the 25 g of vanilla essential oil into a small glass or stainless container.
Weigh the 619 g of olive oil with the 41 g of castor oil added last, and melt the 165 g of coconut oil in 30-second microwave bursts or a double boiler.

Combine all the oils in the mixing jug, add the sugar and the vanilla, and stick blend briefly; both oils and lye should be 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other, warming oils only in a water bath, never the lye in a microwave.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Use the immersion blender in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, leaving a visible trail on the surface.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed 24-48 hours.
Unmold once firm, allowing extra time if soft, and cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Real vanilla browns soap: expect these bars to deepen from cream to tan-brown as they cure — a natural signature, not a flaw.
With nearly 75 percent olive oil, this is a soft-batter recipe; be patient reaching trace and unmolding.
The sugar addition compensates for the low coconut content, keeping the lather lively.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
vanilla-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally; the high-olive base keeps improving for months. Store in a cool, dry place and expect the sweet vanilla scent to deepen with the darkening color.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and the Day-Before Step
steps: The day before soaping, pour coconut milk into an ice cube tray and freeze it solid — frozen milk is what keeps the lye from scorching it.
On soap day, put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 247.5 g coconut oil, 123.8 g shea butter, 41.25 g castor oil, 18 g finely ground dried coconut (or coconut flour), 118 g lye, and your 236 g of liquid as frozen coconut milk (full replacement) or 118 g water plus 118 g coconut milk.

sections.title: Mix the Coconut Milk Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 236 g of coconut milk ice cubes into a heat-resistant container.
Slowly add the 118 g of lye to the frozen milk a little at a time, stirring as the cubes melt and the lye dissolves — the gradual melt keeps the milk sugars from burning.
Stir until fully dissolved and smooth, then set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Ground Coconut
steps: Melt the 247.5 g coconut oil and 123.8 g shea butter to the 38-43°C range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the 18 g of coconut flour or finely ground dried coconut flakes, and stick blend thoroughly.
Check that oils and lye are both between 32-43°C and within a few degrees of each other, adjusting with a warm water bath if needed — never microwave the lye solution.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Optional Fragrance
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring with a long spoon or spatula.
Use the immersion blender until the batter reaches trace, thickening slightly and leaving a visible trail.
If using a coconut fragrance oil, add it now and stir in by hand to avoid accelerating trace, making sure all oil is fully incorporated.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover with a lid or cardboard and wrap in a towel, leaving it undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold once firm and cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Freezing the coconut milk before adding lye is non-negotiable: lye poured into liquid milk scorches its sugars and smells burnt.
Milk soaps run warm, so watch the loaf and keep insulation moderate; some soapers skip insulation entirely for milk batches.
The finely ground coconut adds a mild, tropical exfoliation that matches the bar's theme.

Freeze the milk solid first (ice-cube trays work well), then sprinkle the lye in slowly over the frozen milk, ideally with the container sitting in an ice bath. Lye can push a liquid to around 200 degrees F, and milk sugars scorch at high heat, turning the mixture dark yellow and giving the soap an unpleasant ammonia-like smell that can linger up to 10 days.

If full-milk lye feels risky, use a split method: dissolve the lye in part water (for example half water, half milk, or a water-discounted lye solution), then blend the reserved milk into the batter at trace. This greatly reduces the chance of scorching.

For a light, creamy-colored bar, avoid gel phase: do not cover or insulate a milk soap, and put the mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours after pouring. Milk's natural sugars make the soap heat up, and gel phase darkens milk soaps.
Milk replaces some or all of the recipe water 1:1. If using goat or coconut milk powder instead of fresh milk, BrambleBerry's guideline is about 1 oz of powder per 8 oz of distilled water.
coconut-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the milk-enriched bar is creamy-lathered and keeps well for a year or more.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, with a face mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold, lining a wooden mold with freezer or parchment paper.
Weigh the ingredients: 313 g olive oil, 313 g coconut oil (76 degree), 209 g palm oil, 122 g goat milk, 125 g distilled water, 122 g lye, and 2 teaspoons of honey if using.

sections.title: Mix the Half-Water Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 125 g of distilled water — deliberately only half the total liquid — into a heat-resistant container; the other half enters later as goat milk in the oils.
Slowly add the 122 g of sodium hydroxide to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated and face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F), rewarming only in a warm tap-water bath if it drops too far.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Goat Milk
steps: Weigh the 313 g coconut oil, 313 g olive oil, and 209 g palm oil into a heat-safe container, melting the solid oils in short microwave bursts before adding the olive oil.
Add the 122 g of goat milk to the warm oils and pulse gently with the stick blender to combine milk and oils into a creamy emulsion.
If using, stir in the warmed honey now, and check the mixture is between 32-43°C.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Optional Scent
steps: With both mixtures between 90-110°F and within 10 degrees of each other, slowly pour the lye solution into the milk-and-oil mixture while stirring gently.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until trace — it is easy to over-blend this recipe into too thick a batter, so stop as soon as the trail holds.
If adding essential oils, hand-stir them in now until no unincorporated oil is visible.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold and settle it by gently lifting the mold about a centimeter off the counter and letting it drop a few times.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
Unmold once firm and cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: The split-liquid method — lye in half water, goat milk into the oils — is the easiest way to keep milk from scorching without freezing it.
Milk and honey both heat the loaf, so insulate lightly and check for cracking; many soapers skip insulation for milk soaps entirely.
Goat milk's fats add extra creaminess, so expect a slightly softer bar that rewards a full cure.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
goat-milk-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the nourishing milk bar grows harder and milder as it matures.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, and cover the work area.
Prepare your mold and confirm equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 33.4 g rose (or geranium) essential oil, 2 tablespoons pink clay, 115 g water, 115 g lye, and 115 g coconut milk for the oil phase.

sections.title: Mix the Strong Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 115 g of chilled or frozen distilled water into a heat-resistant container — this is a concentrated half-liquid solution, with the coconut milk making up the rest later.
Carefully add the 115 g of lye to the water, stirring gently; sitting the container in an ice bath helps control the extra heat of this strong mix.
Set aside to cool toward the working range.

sections.title: Blend the Rose Oil and Pink Clay, and Prepare the Oils
steps: Combine the 33.4 g of rose essential oil with the 2 tablespoons of pink clay in a glass container and blend until smooth; set aside.
Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the sugar and the 115 g of coconut milk, and stick blend until creamy, checking both mixtures sit between about 32-43°C and within 10 degrees of each other.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add Rose and Clay
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the milk-and-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend until the batter reaches a light trace only.
Because floral scents accelerate trace, only now add the rose-and-pink-clay mixture, stirring by hand until the color is uniform, with a quick blender burst only if needed.

sections.title: Mold, Crown with Roses, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Let the soap set up slightly, sculpt the top, and press dried rose buds or petals sparingly into the wet surface with a clean spatula or gloved hand — sparse enough that cutting stays easy.
Cover, wrap in a towel, and leave 24-48 hours; unmold once firm and cut into bars.

tips: Add the rose scent only at light trace and by hand; floral fragrances are the classic cause of soap-on-a-stick seizing.
The split liquid — concentrated lye water plus coconut milk in the oils — keeps the milk creamy and unscorched.
Use rose buds on top sparingly so the bars cut cleanly; petals inside the batter would brown.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
rose-soap-with-coconut-milk.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the pink clay holds its blush tone and the rose scent softens romantically with age.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Infusions
steps: Ahead of time, prepare calendula-infused olive oil and brew a calendula tea; chill the tea before soap day.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare the mold with a liner if wooden.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g calendula-infused olive oil, 192 g coconut oil, 167 g shea butter, 58 g cocoa butter, 42 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, half a cup of loosely packed dried calendula flowers, 2 tablespoons kaolin clay, 33.4 g lavender essential oil, 227 g calendula tea, and 113.5 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Calendula Tea Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 227 g of chilled or semi-frozen calendula tea into a heat-safe container and the 113.5 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the tea — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated with your face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); the mask can come off now.

sections.title: Blend the Lavender Clay, and Prepare the Oils
steps: Mix the 33.4 g of lavender essential oil with 2 tablespoons of kaolin clay until smooth and set aside.

Partially melt the 58 g cocoa butter, then add the 192 g coconut oil and 167 g shea butter and warm to the working range; weigh the calendula-infused olive oil, avocado oil, and castor oil (castor last) separately.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug with the sugar, stick blend briefly, and confirm oils and lye are both 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add Petals
steps: Slowly pour the tea-lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter reaches a uniform, slightly thickened trace.
Hand-stir in the lavender-clay mixture until even, then fold in the dried calendula petals and stir to distribute them throughout the batter.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Let it thicken to a toothpaste consistency, sculpt the top, and sprinkle calendula flowers along the middle or one side.
Cover loosely and wrap with a towel; after about 24 hours, when the liner peels cleanly, unmold, then cut into bars once firm.

tips: Calendula is the rare botanical whose petals keep their golden color inside cold process soap instead of browning.
The triple calendula treatment — infused olive oil, tea in the lye, petals at trace — layers the flower's soothing properties throughout the bar.
Cut the loaf on its side so the petal-strewn top does not drag under the knife.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
calendula-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; this healing-herb bar for irritated skin keeps its sunny petals and mildness for a year or more.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Infusions
steps: Ahead of time, make chamomile-infused olive oil and a chamomile infusion for the lye water; cool both.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare the mold with a liner if wooden.

Weigh the ingredients: 418 g chamomile-infused olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 167 g palm oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 25 g chamomile essential oil, 1 tablespoon ground dried chamomile (optional), 2 tablespoons kaolin clay, 235 g chamomile-infused water, 117 g lye, and dried chamomile flowers for the top.

sections.title: Mix the Chamomile Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 235 g of cooled chamomile-infused water into a heat-resistant container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the infusion — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated and face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); the mask can come off once mixed.

sections.title: Blend the Chamomile Clay, and Prepare the Oils
steps: Combine the 25 g of chamomile essential oil, 2 tablespoons of white kaolin clay, and the optional tablespoon of ground dried chamomile; mix well and set aside.
Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 167 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 418 g chamomile-infused olive oil with the 42 g castor oil added last.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug with the sugar and stick blend to unify.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Chamomile Blend
steps: Slowly pour the chamomile lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter reaches trace.
Hand-stir in the chamomile essential oil, clay, and ground chamomile mixture without accelerating trace.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Sprinkle dried chamomile flowers over the top for decoration if desired.
Cover loosely with plastic film or parchment and wrap with a towel; after about 24 hours, unmold when the liner peels away cleanly, and cut into bars once firm.

tips: Chamomile three ways — infused oil, infused lye water, and essential oil in clay — builds a genuinely soothing bar for sensitive skin.
Keep whole chamomile flowers on the top only; inside the bar they would brown.
Kaolin clay anchors the delicate apple-like chamomile scent through the cure.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
chamomile-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; this gentle bar suits nightly use and keeps its calm scent for many months.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Coffee Prep
steps: Ahead of time, prepare coffee-infused olive oil, brew coffee and chill or freeze it into cubes, and make any decorative soap coffee beans.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare the mold with a liner if wooden.
Weigh the ingredients: 418 g coffee-infused olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 167 g palm oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 50 g ground coffee, 235 g cold brewed coffee, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Coffee Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 235 g of chilled, semi-frozen, or frozen coffee into a heat-resistant container and the 117 g of sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the coffee — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved; cold coffee keeps the smell of lye-meets-coffee to a minimum.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F); the mask can come off now.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils
steps: Weigh the 418 g of coffee-infused olive oil with the 42 g of castor oil added last.
Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 167 g palm oil to the same temperature range, then combine all oils in the mixing jug with the sugar and the ground coffee.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the coffee-lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter reaches trace, with the ground coffee evenly suspended.
This recipe relies on coffee itself for scent; if you add any fragrance, hand-stir it in now within IFRA guidelines.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles, decorating the top with soap coffee beans if you made them.
Cover loosely with plastic film or parchment and wrap with a towel for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: Brewed coffee in the lye, coffee-infused oil, and ground coffee in the batter make this a triple-strength kitchen bar that scrubs away garlic and onion odors.
Fresh coffee-lye solution smells odd; the smell vanishes completely during cure.
Use finely ground coffee for gentle exfoliation; coarse grounds can be scratchy on skin.

Use USED (already-brewed) coffee grounds, patted dry on a towel, as the exfoliant. Dry, unbrewed grounds can bleed and leave a brown halo of color in the bar. A good starting rate is about 1 teaspoon of grounds per pound of soap, added at trace; increase from there for a scrubbier bar. Grounds are a large, aggressive exfoliant, best for feet, elbows, and gardener bars.

Strong brewed coffee can replace part or all of the water in the lye solution, but chill it completely (cold or even frozen) before adding lye. Like milk and teas, a warm sugary liquid plus lye heat leads to scorching and off odors; any odd scent in fresh coffee soap fades during cure.

Activated charcoal dosing (The Nerdy Farm Wife's tested table, per pound of oils): 1/8 to 1/2 tsp gives light-to-medium gray soap with white lather; 1 tsp gives dark gray soap with a faint gray lather; 2 tsp to 1 tablespoon gives black soap but noticeably gray lather that can temporarily mark washcloths and soap dishes. Stay at or below about 1 tsp PPO if white lather matters.

Cocoa powder: about 1 teaspoon per pound of soap at light trace yields a medium chocolate brown (start at 1/2 tsp PPO and work up). Always sift and pre-disperse it in a little light oil or water because it clumps, and choose Dutch-process cocoa for a darker, richer brown than natural cocoa.
coffee-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the exfoliating coffee bar is a natural by the kitchen sink and keeps for over a year.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Tea Brewing
steps: Brew strong green tea with 3 tablespoons of loose tea or 3 tea bags steeped at least 5 minutes, strain, and refrigerate or freeze it before soap day.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 232 g chilled brewed green tea, and 115 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Green Tea Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 232 g of frozen or chilled brewed green tea into a heat-resistant container.
Carefully add the 115 g of lye to the green tea — never the reverse — and stir until completely dissolved; cold tea keeps the antioxidants from scorching.
Set aside to cool toward the 32-43°C (90-110°F) working range.

sections.title: Prepare and Combine the Oils
steps: Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last.
Combine the melted and liquid oils in the mixing jug, add the sugar, and stick blend briefly, checking oils and lye are both 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the green tea lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Use the immersion blender in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, thickening slightly and leaving a visible trail on the surface.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Chilled or frozen tea protects the delicate green tea antioxidants from the lye's heat.
Tea-based soaps shift from green toward warm tan during saponification; the antioxidant benefit remains even as the color changes.
This recipe is unscented by design, letting the clean tea character stand alone; any added fragrance should follow IFRA rates.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
green-tea-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place away from direct light to preserve the tea's tone and antioxidant character.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Peppermint Prep
steps: Brew peppermint tea and chill it, and grind dried peppermint leaves to a powder; set both aside.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare the mold with a liner if wooden.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 10 g cane sugar, 56 g peppermint essential oil, 28 g spearmint essential oil, 3 tablespoons French green clay, 1.5 tablespoons ground peppermint leaves, 237 g chilled peppermint tea, and 117 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Peppermint Tea Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the chilled or semi-frozen peppermint tea into a heat-safe container and the sodium hydroxide separately.
Slowly add the lye to the tea — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated with your face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Blend the Mint Oils and Green Clay, and Prepare the Oils
steps: Combine the 56 g of peppermint and 28 g of spearmint essential oils with the 3 tablespoons of French green clay and blend until smooth; set aside.
Weigh the 334 g olive oil, 125 g avocado oil, and 42 g castor oil (castor last); melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter to the working range.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug with the sugar and the ground peppermint leaves.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Mint Clay
steps: Slowly pour the tea-lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in 5-10 second bursts alternating with stirring until the batter reaches a light trace.
Hand-stir in the mint essential oil and green clay mixture until no unincorporated oil remains and the green color is even.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the lined mold and tap gently to release air bubbles.
Cover loosely with plastic film, cardboard, or parchment and wrap with a towel for 18-24 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a stainless steel knife or soap cutter.

tips: The 2:1 peppermint-spearmint pairing gives a rounder mint than peppermint alone, and both oils hold their scent well.
Mint essential oils at this level give a genuinely icy skin feel — invigorating in summer, intense in winter; adjust future batches to taste.
Peppermint tea in the lye plus ground leaves in the batter add color depth and mild exfoliation to back up the scent.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.
peppermint-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the invigorating mint stays strong for a year, making this a dependable wake-up shower bar.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Rosemary Tea
steps: At least four hours ahead, pour 280 g of simmering water over 2 tablespoons of rosemary needles, steep 20 minutes, strain, and chill the tea.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 232 g chilled rosemary tea, 115 g lye, 3 tablespoons kaolin clay, 56 g rosemary essential oil, and 28 g lemon essential oil.

sections.title: Blend the Rosemary-Lemon Clay Mixture
steps: Add the 3 tablespoons of kaolin clay to a clean, dry glass or stainless container.
Weigh in the 56 g of rosemary and 28 g of lemon essential oils, stir well, and set aside so the ingredients marry.

sections.title: Mix the Rosemary Tea Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 232 g of chilled rosemary tea into a heat-resistant container, topping up with distilled water if short.
Carefully add the 115 g of lye to the tea — never the reverse — stirring until completely dissolved, then set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last, then combine all oils in the mixing jug and stick blend briefly, confirming both mixtures are 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other.
Slowly pour the tea-lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously, then stick blend until the batter reaches trace.
Hand-stir in the rosemary-lemon clay mixture until fully combined.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently to release air bubbles, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Rosemary tea in the lye water plus rosemary essential oil doubles down on the herb's stimulating, toning character.
The lemon brightens the opening of the scent but will fade first, leaving a cleanly herbal rosemary bar.
A sprig of dried rosemary pressed along the top makes an attractive, functional label for the loaf.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
rosemary-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; rosemary is among the most persistent herbal scents and keeps this bar smelling fresh for a year.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare the mold with a liner if wooden.
Check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum, and have a chopstick ready for the swirl.

Weigh the ingredients: 334 g olive oil, 209 g coconut oil, 125 g shea butter, 125 g avocado oil, 42 g castor oil, 116 g aloe vera juice, 10 g cane sugar, 3 tablespoons French green clay, 56 g eucalyptus essential oil, 28 g spearmint essential oil, 1 teaspoon indigo powder, 116 g water, and 116 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Concentrated Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 116 g of chilled or semi-frozen water into a heat-safe container — the aloe juice provides the rest of the liquid later, in the oils.
Slowly add the 116 g of sodium hydroxide to the water — never the reverse — stirring until dissolved, ventilated with your face turned away.
Set aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).

sections.title: Prepare the Clay, Indigo, and Oils
steps: Blend the 56 g eucalyptus and 28 g spearmint essential oils with 3 tablespoons of French green clay until smooth; separately mix the teaspoon of indigo powder with a tablespoon of hot water; set both aside.
Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 125 g shea butter to the working range; weigh the 334 g olive oil, 125 g avocado oil, and 42 g castor oil (castor last).
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the sugar and the 116 g of aloe vera juice, and stick blend to a smooth emulsion.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Split for the Indigo Swirl
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the aloe-and-oil mixture while stirring, then stick blend in short bursts to a light trace.
Hand-stir in the eucalyptus-spearmint clay mixture until the green is even, then pour off half a cup of batter into the hydrated indigo container and stir it well to make the blue portion.

sections.title: Pour the Swirl, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour half the green batter into the mold, add the indigo batter without scraping its container, then pour the remaining green batter on top.
Swirl a chopstick in circles down the length of the mold, stripe any leftover indigo across the top, and curl the tip a quarter-inch deep to marble both colors; tap the mold to settle it.
Cover loosely, wrap with a towel, and after 18-24 hours unmold when the liner peels cleanly, then cut into bars once firm.

tips: The split-liquid trick — strong lye water plus aloe juice in the oils — preserves the aloe's soothing qualities.
Do not scrape the indigo container when pouring; the last dregs cause streaks instead of clean blue ribbons.
Keep the swirl shallow on top and bold inside so every cut bar shows a different green-and-blue wave.

Start with 1 teaspoon of clay per pound (454 g) of soaping oils; Lovely Greens' example clay bars are all made at exactly this rate, and 1-2 tsp per pound is the usual working range for French green clay.

Add clay as a slurry, not a dry powder: pre-mix it with three times its volume of distilled water (five times for smectite clays) before adding at trace. This extra water stops the clay from clumping, accelerating trace, or cracking the finished bars, and many soapmakers hydrate the slurry several hours ahead so it turns smooth and fluid.

Clay is one of the most stable natural soap colorants: its colors survive saponification and don't fade or morph during cure the way plant-based colorants do, so a French green clay bar keeps its sage-green color long-term.

Leaf-based green powders (spirulina, nettle, matcha, spinach and similar) fade toward yellow in ordinary daylight; cure and store those bars in the dark to slow the fade. For a natural green that actually lasts, Lovely Greens recommends alfalfa powder, or lean on the mineral stability of French green clay.
aloe-vera-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the aloe-and-mint bar is at its soothing, cooling best within the first year.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and De-Alcoholized Beer
steps: At least one day ahead, simmer about 500 g of beer uncovered for at least 20 minutes to boil off the alcohol, then refrigerate or freeze it.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 232 g of the boiled-then-chilled beer, 115 g lye, 3 tablespoons kaolin clay, and the essential oils — 40 g grapefruit, 28 g lemon, and 10 g patchouli.

sections.title: Blend the Essential Oil and Clay Mixture
steps: Add the 3 tablespoons of kaolin clay to a clean, dry glass or stainless container.
Weigh in the grapefruit, lemon, and patchouli essential oils, stir well, and set aside to marry.

sections.title: Mix the Beer Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 232 g of frozen or chilled de-alcoholized beer into a heat-resistant container, topping up with chilled distilled water if short.
Add the 115 g of lye crystals a little at a time — never liquid onto lye — stirring so the frozen beer melts as the lye dissolves; the gradual addition keeps the sugary beer from foaming over.
Stir until completely dissolved and set aside; the mask can come off now.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last, then combine all oils in the mixing jug and stick blend briefly.
Slowly pour the beer-lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend until the batter reaches trace.
Add the essential oil and clay mixture and stir well with a spatula or whisk to combine completely.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently to release air bubbles, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly after 18-24 hours or more, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Never skip boiling off the alcohol — live alcohol meeting lye foams violently; flat, chilled beer behaves.
Beer sugars boost lather and can speed trace, so add the lye slowly and watch the batter.
Fresh beer soap can smell yeasty, but the recipe's own note is right: it improves significantly within a week of cure.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible.
