Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
beer-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally; any brewery note fades early in the cure, leaving the citrus-patchouli blend. Store in a cool, dry place.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Simmered Wine
steps: At least one day ahead, simmer 280 g of red wine uncovered for at least 20 minutes to drive off the alcohol, then refrigerate or freeze it.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 412.5 g olive oil, 206.25 g coconut oil, 165 g palm oil, 41.25 g castor oil, 232 g of the boiled-then-frozen red wine, 115 g lye, 3 tablespoons kaolin clay, and the essential oils — 40 g grapefruit, 28 g rosemary, and 10 g patchouli.

sections.title: Blend the Essential Oil and Clay Mixture
steps: Add the 3 tablespoons of kaolin clay to a clean, dry glass or stainless container.
Weigh in the grapefruit, rosemary, and patchouli essential oils, stir well, and set aside to marry.

sections.title: Mix the Red Wine Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 232 g of frozen or chilled simmered wine into a heat-resistant container, topping up with chilled distilled water if needed.
Add the 115 g of lye crystals a little at a time, stirring so the frozen wine melts as the lye dissolves — slow addition stops the wine's sugars from scorching and foaming.
Stir until completely dissolved and set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Combine and Trace
steps: Melt the 206.25 g coconut oil and 165 g palm oil to the working range; weigh the 412.5 g olive oil with the 41.25 g castor oil added last, then combine all oils in the mixing jug, stick blend briefly, and confirm both mixtures are 32-43°C and within about 5°C of each other.
Slowly pour the wine-lye solution into the oils while stirring, then stick blend until the batter reaches trace.
Add the essential oil and clay mixture and stir well with a spatula or whisk to combine completely.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: Boiling off the wine's alcohol before it meets lye is essential; alcohol plus lye erupts in foam.
Expect earthy rose-to-mauve tones rather than wine purple, as red wine pigments shift in high-pH soap.
The polyphenol-rich wine plus grapefruit-rosemary-patchouli blend makes a sophisticated, spa-style bar worth labeling proudly.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
red-wine-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally; any winey sharpness mellows during the first weeks. Store in a cool, dry place.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Applesauce
steps: Buy unsweetened (baby-food style) applesauce or make your own: peel, core, and chop apples, barely cover with water, bring just to a simmer, steam 15 minutes off the heat, then puree smooth and chill.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the ingredients: 443 g olive oil, 167 g coconut oil, 167 g shea butter, 58.45 g castor oil, 100 g chilled applesauce, 150 g distilled water, and 113 g lye.

sections.title: Mix a Cool Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the 150 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container.
Carefully add the 113 g of lye — never the reverse — stirring until completely dissolved.
Let it cool to the deliberately low 29-32°C (85-90°F) range, which offsets the extra heat the applesauce sugars will generate.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Applesauce
steps: Weigh the 443 g of olive oil with the 58.45 g of castor oil added last; melt the 167 g coconut oil and 167 g shea butter to the same cool range.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug and stir well, then add the 100 g of applesauce and stick blend until the mixture is completely smooth before any lye goes in.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the cool lye solution into the apple-and-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, proceeding cautiously — the fruit sugars can accelerate trace.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently to release air bubbles, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels away cleanly after 18-24 hours or more, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

tips: The cool 29-32°C soaping temperature is this recipe's guardrail against the applesauce sugars overheating the loaf.
Use unsweetened applesauce only; added sugar magnifies overheating and darkening.
Fruit purees count as liquid, so this recipe already reduces the water — do not add extra.

Formulate salt bars with 50-100% of the oil weight in fine-grain sea salt (beginners start at 50%) and a coconut-oil-heavy base with a high superfat, because salt suppresses lather; Soap Queen's salt bar runs 50% coconut oil and many formulas go 80-100% coconut with 15-20% superfat.

Cut salt bars EARLY, in hours not days: salt makes the batter harden extremely fast, so a loaf must be unmolded and cut as soon as it is firm, roughly 1-6 hours after pouring depending on the recipe. Wait overnight and the loaf crumbles when cut. Individual cavity molds sidestep the timing problem entirely.

Use plain fine sea salt or Himalayan pink salt, not Dead Sea salt or Epsom salt. Dead Sea salt's very high mineral content is strongly hygroscopic, pulling moisture from the air and producing weepy, sweaty, soft bars.

Add fruit or vegetable purees at thin trace. Sugary purees (strawberry, banana, mango) speed up trace and heat the soap, so soap at cooler temperatures, skip insulation, and refrigerate or freeze the mold after pouring, since overheated sugar can crack, volcano, or caramelize the bar to a dull brown.
apple-soap.cure_and_storage: Dry the bars on a rack in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks, turning occasionally. Store in a cool, dry place; the fruit-enriched bar is best enjoyed within a year.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Avocado Puree
steps: Peel and pit a ripe avocado, weigh out 100 g of flesh, and puree it perfectly smooth with the stick blender, using small amounts of the weighed 376 g of olive oil to help it blend — the rest of that olive oil joins the main batch.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.
Weigh the remaining ingredients: 209 g coconut oil, 108 g shea butter, 108 g avocado oil, 33 g castor oil, 1 teaspoon granulated sugar, 41.75 g lemongrass essential oil, 115 g water, and 115 g lye.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution and the Clay Blend
steps: Weigh the 115 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container, carefully add the 115 g of lye — never the reverse — stir until dissolved, and set aside.
In a small container, mix the 41.75 g of lemongrass essential oil with 1 tablespoon each of yellow clay, French green clay, and white kaolin clay; set aside to hydrate.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Avocado
steps: Melt the 209 g coconut oil and 108 g shea butter to the cool 29-32°C (85-90°F) range; combine the remaining olive oil from the puree step with the 108 g avocado oil and the 33 g castor oil added last.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the avocado-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, thickening slightly and leaving a visible trail.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold

When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

Both avocado flesh and avocado oil enrich this bar, so a full cure matters for hardness.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Peach Puree
steps: Make or buy unsweetened peach puree and chill it.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and check equipment is clean, dry, and non-aluminum.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils, Puree and Color
steps: Weigh the 443 g olive oil with the 58.45 g castor oil added last; melt the 167 g coconut oil and 167 g shea butter to the same cool range.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the 100 g of peach puree, scrape in the hydrated yellow clay and turmeric mixture, and stick blend until completely smooth.

sections.title: Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Slowly pour the cool lye solution into the peach-and-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend in short bursts until the batter reaches trace, watching carefully — the peach sugars can accelerate it.

Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Spice-Infused Oil
steps: Ahead of time, weigh 500 g of olive oil into a lidded glass container with 2 whole allspice berries (or 1 teaspoon ground) and 1 nutmeg (or 1 teaspoon ground), warm gently, and infuse for at least 2 hours.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, mask for the lye stage, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 443 g of the strained spice-infused olive oil, 167 g coconut oil, 167 g shea butter, 58.45 g castor oil, 100 g pumpkin puree, 150 g distilled water, 113 g lye, plus 5 g cinnamon leaf essential oil, 5 g clove bud essential oil, 28 g spice-infused olive oil, 2 tablespoons yellow clay, and 1.5 teaspoons turmeric for the spice-color blend.

sections.title: Mix a Cool Lye Solution and the Spice-Clay Blend
steps: Weigh the 150 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container, carefully add the 113 g of lye — never the reverse — stir until dissolved, and cool to 29-32°C (85-90°F) to offset the pumpkin's sugars; the mask can come off once mixed.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Pumpkin
steps: Strain and weigh the 443 g of spice-infused olive oil with the 58.45 g of castor oil added last; melt the 167 g coconut oil and 167 g shea butter to the same cool range.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the 100 g of pumpkin puree, and stick blend until smooth before the lye goes in.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Spices
steps: Slowly pour the cool lye solution into the pumpkin-and-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend to a light trace only, since the pumpkin sugars accelerate thickening.
Hand-whisk in the spice, clay, and turmeric mixture — cinnamon and clove are famous trace accelerators, so stir deliberately and use only a quick blender burst if needed to finish.

steps: Pour the autumn-colored batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

Infusing the whole spices into the olive oil layers in warmth without gritty spice particles.

sections.title: Safety, Setup and Strawberry Puree
steps: Make or buy unsweetened strawberry puree — blitzing thawed unsweetened frozen strawberries perfectly smooth works well — and chill it.
Put on safety goggles and gloves, cover the work area, and prepare your mold.

Weigh the ingredients: 443 g olive oil, 167 g coconut oil, 167 g shea butter, 58.45 g castor oil, 100 g strawberry puree, 150 g distilled water, 113 g lye, plus 40 g grapefruit, 28 g bergamot, and 28 g lemongrass essential oils, 2 tablespoons rose clay, 1.5 teaspoons paprika, and an optional teaspoon of poppy seeds.

sections.title: Mix a Cool Lye Solution and the Berry-Clay Blend
steps: Weigh the 150 g of frozen or chilled distilled water into a heat-resistant container, carefully add the 113 g of lye — never the reverse — stir until dissolved, and cool to 29-32°C (85-90°F) to offset the berry sugars.
Combine the grapefruit, bergamot, and lemongrass essential oils with the rose clay and paprika and blend until smooth; set aside.

sections.title: Prepare the Oils and Strawberries
steps: Weigh the 443 g olive oil with the 58.45 g castor oil added last; melt the 167 g coconut oil and 167 g shea butter to the same cool range.
Combine all oils in the mixing jug, add the 100 g of strawberry puree and the optional poppy seeds, and stick blend until smooth.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Clay Blend
steps: Slowly pour the cool lye solution into the strawberry-and-oil mixture while stirring continuously.
Stick blend to a light trace, staying cautious as the berry sugars accelerate thickening.
Hand-stir in the essential oil, rose clay, and paprika mixture until the pink is even, finishing with a quick blender burst only if needed.

sections.title: Mold, Insulate and Unmold
steps: Pour the pink batter into the mold, lining a wooden mold with parchment first, tap gently, and decorate the top as desired.
Cover with a lid or cardboard, wrap in a towel, and leave undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
When the liner peels cleanly, unmold; once firm, cut into bars with a knife or soap cutter.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on gloves, goggles, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, and work outdoors or in a well-ventilated room away from children and pets.
Set out a sensitive digital scale, a non-aluminum pot, a heat-safe lye container, stirring utensils, and silicone molds around 10x10 cm.

Weigh the ingredients: 500 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, 100 g cocoa butter, 150 g sodium hydroxide, 350 ml distilled water, and the optional extras — 20 ml lavender essential oil, 2 tablespoons rose petals, 1 tablespoon sage, and 2 tablespoons oatmeal — then run the recipe through a lye calculator to confirm the lye amount for your exact oils before starting.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the 500 g olive oil, 200 g coconut oil, and 100 g cocoa butter together in a pot over low heat, following this recipe's oils-first order.
Bring the oils to 40-50°C, stir until fully combined, and turn off the heat.

sections.title: Mix the Lye Solution
steps: In a separate heat-safe container, carefully add the 150 g of sodium hydroxide to the 350 ml of distilled water — never water onto lye — stirring gently as it heats.
Ensure good ventilation, keep your face away from the fumes, and let the solution cool.

sections.title: Combine and Add the Garden Botanicals
steps: Slowly blend the cooled sodium hydroxide solution into the melted oils, keeping the mixture between 35-45°C, and stir thoroughly until smooth and emulsified.
Add the optional lavender essential oil, rose petals, sage, and oatmeal, and mix the ingredients thoroughly through the batter.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, Cut with a Hot Knife, and Rest
steps: Pour the mixture into the silicone molds; as you pour, decorate the tops with rose petals or sage leaves, and optionally sprinkle oatmeal for a textured, abstract surface — a few lavender flowers on top complete the garden look.
Let the molds sit at room temperature for a few days until the soap is firm, keeping gloves on for any handling.
Remove the bars and cut them into desired shapes using a knife dipped in hot water, the Japanese-style trick for clean, glassy cuts.

tips: The hot-water-soaked knife is this technique's signature: heat the blade, wipe it, and slice for clean edges.
Keep most botanicals on the surface; petals and herbs mixed deep into the bar tend to brown over time.
Because this book's recipes state generous lye amounts, verifying 150 g against a lye calculator for these exact oils is an essential safety step.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-garden-soap.cure_and_storage: After cutting, let the bars cure in a well-ventilated, cool, dry place for a few weeks — 4-6 weeks gives the mildest, hardest bar. Store cured soap in an airy spot out of direct sunlight.

sections.title: Mix the Lavender-Water Lye Solution
steps: With your face averted, slowly sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the cooled lavender-infused water, stirring with a silicone spoon until fully dissolved — never the reverse order.
Label the solution and let it cool in a safe spot for 30-40 minutes; the herbal infusion may darken, which is normal and will not harm the finished soap.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and sweet almond oil together over low heat, bring them to 40-50°C, and turn off the heat.
Pre-mix the purple mica with a spoonful of the warm oils, and loosen the 5 grams of honey with a teaspoon of warm water so both incorporate without clumping or hot spots.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Lavender Extras
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution down the stick blender shaft into the oils and pulse in short bursts until the batter reaches a thin trace.
Blend in the lavender essential oil, the purple mica slurry, and the diluted honey, working quickly since honey can speed trace.
Reserve most of the dried lavender buds for decorating the tops, as buds mixed through the bar can discolor.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into silicone molds, tap them on the counter to release air, and sprinkle the lavender buds over the surface.
Because of the honey, do not insulate the molds — sugar-fed batter overheats easily; leave them uncovered at room temperature for a few days.
Unmold once firm and cut the bars into desired shapes using a knife dipped in hot water, keeping gloves on for fresh soap.

tips: Honey accelerates trace and heats the batter, so add it at the lightest trace you can and skip any insulation.
Dissolve the purple mica in oil before trace-time; dry mica dumped into batter leaves streaks and specks.
Lavender essential oil is one of the best-behaved oils in cold process — a good recipe for beginners to practice fragrance timing.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-fields-soap-variation-2.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars spaced apart in a well-ventilated, dim, dry spot for a few weeks — 4-6 weeks is standard — then store them with airflow rather than in sealed plastic so the lavender scent stays clean.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Wear splash goggles, nitrile gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes throughout, and work at a ventilated sink with no children or pets in the room.
Squeeze and chill the 350 ml of lemon juice ahead of time — cold juice keeps the lye reaction calmer and protects the fresh citrus character.

Weigh the 450 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of cocoa butter, and 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and stage the optional 20 grams of lemon essential oil, 15 grams of lemon zest, 10 grams of turmeric powder, and 5 grams of poppy seeds.

sections.title: Mix the Lemon Juice Lye Solution
steps: Sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the chilled lemon juice a little at a time with your face turned away; the citric acid makes the mixture fizz and heat more vigorously than plain water, so go slowly and stir between each addition.
Stir until fully dissolved, label the container, and let the solution cool in a safe, ventilated spot away from children and pets.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and cocoa butter together over low heat, bring the blend to 40-50°C, and turn off the heat.
Disperse the turmeric powder in a spoonful of the warm oils now so it colors the batter evenly, and let everything settle toward the recipe's 35-45°C combining range.

sections.title: Bring to Trace and Add the Sunshine Extras
steps: Pour the cooled lemon-lye solution slowly down the stick blender shaft into the oils and pulse in short bursts, hand-stirring between pulses, until you reach a thin, uniform trace.
Blend in the lemon essential oil for fragrance, the lemon zest for gentle exfoliation, the turmeric slurry for its sunny yellow color, and the poppy seeds for speckled texture.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into silicone molds, tap them firmly to knock out air pockets, and smooth or texture the tops.
Let the molds sit at room temperature for a few days while saponification finishes, handling only with gloves.
Unmold the firm bars and cut them into desired shapes with a knife dipped in hot water.

tips: Expect fizzing when lye meets lemon juice — it is the citric acid reacting; slow additions and a deep pitcher keep it contained.
Poppy seeds sink in thin batter, so bring the trace slightly past thin before adding them if you want even speckles.
Citrus essential oil fades during cure; lemon zest and turmeric carry the sunshine theme even as the scent softens.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
lemon-sunshine-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars in a well-ventilated, dim, dry area for a few weeks — 4-6 weeks gives the hardest, mildest bar — then store with airflow out of direct sunlight to preserve the yellow color.

Brew a strong chamomile infusion and cool it fully — the 350 ml of chamomile-infused water must be cool before it ever meets lye.

Weigh the 450 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of shea butter, and 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and stage the optional 20 grams of chamomile essential oil, 15 grams of dried chamomile flowers, 10 grams of calendula oil, and 5 grams of honey.

sections.title: Mix the Chamomile Lye Solution
steps: Slowly sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the cooled chamomile-infused water, stirring until fully dissolved, with your face turned away from the fumes.
Set the labeled solution aside to cool in a safe spot; the golden infusion will darken but the soothing plant compounds remain.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and shea butter in a pot over low heat, holding the temperature between 40-50°C as the recipe directs.
Loosen the 5 grams of honey with a teaspoon of warm water so it disperses without creating a hot spot in the batter.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Garden Extras
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the melted oils while stirring continuously, then switch to short stick blender bursts until the batter reaches a thin, streak-free trace.
Stir in the chamomile essential oil for its calming fragrance, the calendula oil for its skin-soothing properties, and the diluted honey for extra moisture.
Reserve the dried chamomile flowers for the surface of the loaf so they stay golden instead of browning inside the bar.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap out air bubbles, and decorate the tops with the dried chamomile flowers.
Because of the honey, leave the molds uninsulated at room temperature and let the soap sit for 24-48 hours as the recipe specifies.
Once set, unmold with gloves on and cut the loaf into desired shapes.

tips: Adding the calendula oil at trace preserves more of its soothing character than melting it with the base oils.
Honey batters run hot — skip the towel wrap and watch for a center crack, moving the mold somewhere cooler if one appears.

tranquil-garden-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars in a well-ventilated area for 4-6 weeks as the recipe directs, turning them occasionally so all sides dry evenly, then store in a dim, dry spot with airflow.

steps: Dress in goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, and set up in a ventilated kitchen free of children and pets.
Prepare the orange-infused water in advance and cool it completely before the lye stage.

Weigh the 400 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of sweet almond oil, 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and 350 ml of cooled orange-infused water, plus the optional 20 grams of sweet orange essential oil, 15 grams of lemon zest, 10 grams of vitamin E oil, and 5 grams of turmeric powder.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Citrus Extras

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap them firmly to release trapped air, and smooth the tops.
Let the soap rest in the molds at room temperature for 24-48 hours as the recipe specifies, handling only with gloves.
Once set, unmold and cut into desired shapes while the loaf is still easy to slice.

tips: Sweet orange essential oil fades faster than most during cure — anchor the theme with the zest and turmeric color, or slightly favor the orange oil within the stated amounts.
Zest distributes best at a light-to-medium trace; too thin and it sinks, too thick and it clumps.
An isopropyl alcohol spritz after pouring keeps soda ash from clouding the citrus colors.

refreshing-citrus-burst-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a well-ventilated, dim, dry spot as the recipe directs, then store them with airflow away from sunlight, which fades citrus color and scent fastest.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on splash goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, and clear the ventilated workspace of children and pets.
Steep cedarwood chips in hot water ahead of time, strain, and cool the infusion completely to make the 350 ml of cedarwood-infused water.

Weigh the 450 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of shea butter, and 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and stage the optional 20 grams of cedarwood essential oil, 15 grams of dried cedarwood chips, 10 grams of activated charcoal, and 5 grams of tea tree essential oil.

sections.title: Mix the Cedarwood Lye Solution
steps: Slowly sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the cooled cedarwood-infused water, stirring until every granule dissolves, with your face turned away.
Set the labeled solution in a safe spot to cool toward the working range.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and shea butter over low heat, holding the blend between 40-50°C.
Disperse the 10 grams of activated charcoal in a spoonful of the warm oils so it blends in as smooth gray-black rather than gritty specks.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Woodsy Extras
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the melted oils while stirring continuously, then bring the batter to a thin trace with short stick blender bursts.
Blend in the cedarwood essential oil for the forest fragrance, the tea tree essential oil for its cleansing bite, and the charcoal slurry for a deep woodsy color.
Reserve the dried cedarwood chips for the tops of the bars — chips inside the bar are scratchy in use, but on top they are handsome decoration.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap out the air pockets, and press the cedarwood chips lightly into the surface.
Let the soap sit in the molds at room temperature for 24-48 hours, using gloves for any handling.
Unmold once firm and cut into desired shapes; charcoal soap cuts cleanest with a wire or a hot knife.

tips: Charcoal lather can gray a light washcloth at higher doses; the modest 10 grams here keeps the bar dark but the lather tame.
Cedarwood and tea tree are both well-behaved in cold process, making this a forgiving batch for practicing color work.
Wipe your cutter between slices so the charcoal core does not smear across the lighter edges.

Use USED (already-brewed) coffee grounds, patted dry on a towel, as the exfoliant. Dry, unbrewed grounds can bleed and leave a brown halo of color in the bar. A good starting rate is about 1 teaspoon of grounds per pound of soap, added at trace; increase from there for a scrubbier bar. Grounds are a large, aggressive exfoliant, best for feet, elbows, and gardener bars.

Strong brewed coffee can replace part or all of the water in the lye solution, but chill it completely (cold or even frozen) before adding lye. Like milk and teas, a warm sugary liquid plus lye heat leads to scorching and off odors; any odd scent in fresh coffee soap fades during cure.

Activated charcoal dosing (The Nerdy Farm Wife's tested table, per pound of oils): 1/8 to 1/2 tsp gives light-to-medium gray soap with white lather; 1 tsp gives dark gray soap with a faint gray lather; 2 tsp to 1 tablespoon gives black soap but noticeably gray lather that can temporarily mark washcloths and soap dishes. Stay at or below about 1 tsp PPO if white lather matters.

Cocoa powder: about 1 teaspoon per pound of soap at light trace yields a medium chocolate brown (start at 1/2 tsp PPO and work up). Always sift and pre-disperse it in a little light oil or water because it clumps, and choose Dutch-process cocoa for a darker, richer brown than natural cocoa.
woodsy-cedar-haven-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a ventilated, dim, dry space, turning occasionally, then store with airflow; the cedar scent deepens and rounds out as the bars age.

sections.title: Mix the Lavender Lye Solution

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and shea butter over low heat, maintaining 40-50°C per the recipe.
Pre-mix the purple mica in a spoonful of warm oil and loosen the 10 grams of honey with warm water so both blend in smoothly at trace.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Dream Extras
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the melted oils while stirring continuously, then pulse the stick blender in short bursts to a thin trace.
Blend in the lavender essential oil and vanilla extract for the signature scent, the almond oil and diluted honey for extra moisture, and the purple mica slurry for a soft violet hue.
Know that vanilla naturally browns soap over time — the purple may drift toward mauve, which is part of this bar's dreamy character.
Reserve the dried lavender buds for the tops rather than mixing them through.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap out air bubbles, and finish the tops with the lavender buds.
Skip insulation because of the honey, and let the molds rest at room temperature for 24-48 hours.
Unmold once firm, gloves on, and cut the bars into desired shapes.

Honey plus vanilla means extra sugar in the batter — keep it uninsulated and check for overheating cracks in the first day.
Lavender-vanilla scent matures beautifully during cure; resist judging the fragrance before week four.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, ventilate the space, and remove children and pets from the room.
Chill the 350 ml of oat milk until very cold or slushy — milk sugars scorch when lye heats the liquid.

Weigh the 400 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of almond oil, and 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and stage the optional 20 grams of almond essential oil, 20 grams of honey, 20 grams of colloidal oatmeal, 15 grams of crushed almonds, 10 grams of shea butter, and 5 grams of vitamin E oil.

sections.title: Mix the Oat Milk Lye Solution
steps: Sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the cold oat milk a spoonful at a time, stirring between additions with your face turned away; slow additions keep the milk from scorching and turning orange.
Stir until fully dissolved and set the labeled solution aside to cool — a creamy tan color is normal.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and almond oil together with the 10 grams of shea butter over low heat, maintaining 40-50°C.
Loosen the honey with a teaspoon of warm water and have the colloidal oatmeal and crushed almonds ready beside the pot.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Delight Extras
steps: Slowly pour the oat milk lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously, then pulse the stick blender in short bursts to a thin trace.

Blend in the almond essential oil for fragrance, the diluted honey for its antibacterial sweetness, the colloidal oatmeal for gentle exfoliation, the crushed almonds for texture, and the vitamin E oil for skin nourishment.
Work quickly once the honey goes in — sugars can accelerate trace.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the thickening batter into molds, tap firmly to release air, and texture the tops if you like.
Do not insulate — oat milk plus honey is a high-sugar combination that overheats and cracks when wrapped; leave the molds uncovered at cool room temperature for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves once firm and cut into desired shapes.

tips: This is a double-sugar recipe (oat milk and honey): soap it cool, skip the towel wrap, and consider refrigerating the mold for the first day.
Colloidal oatmeal disperses without grit; the crushed almonds carry the scrub factor, so size them to your preference before trace.
If the oat milk lye smells strong while mixing, keep going — the odor vanishes during cure.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
honey-oatmeal-almond-delight-soap.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a ventilated, dim, dry spot, turning occasionally, then store with airflow; milk-and-honey bars reward a full cure with an especially creamy lather.

sections.title: Mix the Orange Juice Lye Solution
steps: Sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the chilled orange juice a little at a time with your face turned away; the juice sugars and acids make the reaction livelier and darker than plain water, so add slowly and stir constantly.

sections.title: Melt the Oils

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Spice Extras
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the melted oils while stirring continuously, then bring the batter to a thin trace with short stick blender bursts.
Blend in the orange and cinnamon essential oils, then the spice slurry of clove, ginger, and cardamom for the warm, exotic scent.
Move promptly to the mold — cinnamon and clove are known trace accelerators, and the batter will thicken fast once they are in.
Reserve the dried orange peel for decorating the tops.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap out air pockets, and press the dried orange peel onto the surface.
Skip heavy insulation — juice sugars plus warming spices run hot; let the molds sit at room temperature for 24-48 hours.
Unmold with gloves once set and cut into desired shapes.

tips: Cinnamon and clove essential oils are strong skin sensitizers and fast trace accelerators — have the mold ready before you blend them in.
Orange juice in the lye adds natural sugars: expect a darker batter and keep the mold cool to prevent cracking.
The spice powders give a natural tan-gold gradient; stirring them in unevenly on purpose creates a handsome swirl.

sections.title: Safety and Setup
steps: Put on goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes, and work in a ventilated kitchen cleared of children and pets.
Brew strong green tea in advance and chill it — the 350 ml of green tea must be fully cooled before mixing with lye.

Weigh the 400 grams of olive oil, 250 grams of coconut oil, 150 grams of avocado oil, and 200 grams of sodium hydroxide, and stage the optional 20 grams of aloe vera gel, 20 grams of green tea extract, 15 grams of cucumber seed oil, 10 grams of peppermint essential oil, and 5 grams of spirulina powder.

sections.title: Mix the Green Tea Lye Solution
steps: Slowly sprinkle the sodium hydroxide into the cooled green tea, stirring until fully dissolved, with your face turned away; the tea will darken to amber-brown, which is normal.
Label the solution and set it aside to cool in a safe spot.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the olive oil, coconut oil, and avocado oil together over low heat, maintaining the recipe's 40-50°C range.
Disperse the spirulina powder in a spoonful of warm oil for an even green, and have the aloe vera gel, green tea extract, and cucumber seed oil measured beside the pot.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Soothing Extras
steps: Slowly pour the lye solution into the oils while stirring continuously, then pulse the stick blender in short bursts until a thin trace forms.

Blend in the aloe vera gel and green tea extract for their soothing properties, the cucumber seed oil for hydration, the peppermint essential oil for its cool, refreshing scent, and the spirulina slurry for a natural green color.

sections.title: Mold, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds, tap firmly to release air bubbles, and smooth the tops.
Let the soap rest in the molds at room temperature for 24-48 hours, handling only with gloves.
Unmold once firm and cut into desired shapes.

tips: Spirulina gives a sage-to-forest green that fades in sunlight — cure and store these bars somewhere dim to keep the color.
Adding the aloe gel at trace rather than to the lye water preserves more of its soothing polysaccharides.
Peppermint at this modest dose cools without stinging, making the bar genuinely refreshing for summer showers.

Set the labeled solution aside to cool for 30-40 minutes.

sections.title: Melt the Oils
steps: Melt the coconut oil gently and stir in the olive oil.
Bring both oils and lye toward 90-110°F before combining.

sections.title: Combine, Trace, and Add the Citrus-Mint Blend
steps: Pour the cooled lye down the stick blender shaft into the oils and pulse in short bursts until the batter traces.
Add the grapefruit, lemongrass, and peppermint essential oils — the recipe's stated trio — and stir thoroughly.

sections.title: Mold, Decorate, Set, and Unmold
steps: Pour the batter into molds and tap out the bubbles.
Scatter the dried grapefruit zest, lemongrass, and mint leaves across the tops — this variation's fuller three-part garnish.
Let the soap set for 24 hours, then unmold and cut into bars.

tips: This variation is distinguished by its triple botanical topping — chop the lemongrass finely so the cut bars stay tidy.
Lemongrass is the endurance runner of the blend, still fragrant when the grapefruit has faded.
Cure and store in the dark: light bleaches both the zest garnish and the citrus scent.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
grapefruit-lemongrass-peppermint-soap-va.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a ventilated, dim, dry area, then store with airflow away from sunlight to protect the bright citrus-mint profile.

Sprinkle the dried lavender buds, rosemary leaves, and thyme leaves across the tops.

tips: Thyme essential oil is strong and slightly medicinal — its 10 gram position keeps the blend aromatic rather than clinical.
All three of these herbs behave well at trace, making this a low-drama batch for practicing herb-topped finishes.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
lavender-rosemary-thyme-soap-variation-2.cure_and_storage: Cure the bars for 4-6 weeks in a well-ventilated, dim, dry spot, turning occasionally, then store with airflow so the herbal trio stays true.

sections.title: Sanitize and Measure
steps: Spray your heat-safe bowl, spatula, and the final jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air-dry — clean tools are what keep an oil-based butter fresh for months.
Measure the 1/4 cup of cocoa butter, 1/4 cup of coconut oil, and 2 tablespoons of sweet almond oil into the heat-safe bowl.
Set the 10 drops of orange essential oil and 5 drops of vanilla essential oil beside the stove for the cool-down stage.

sections.title: Melt over a Double Boiler
steps: Place the bowl over a pot with an inch or two of simmering water to create a gentle double boiler — direct stovetop heat can scorch cocoa butter.
Stir until the cocoa butter, coconut oil, and sweet almond oil are fully melted and well combined into one clear golden liquid.
Use pot holders and keep the bowl steady; hot oils scald.

sections.title: Cool Down and Add the Dream Scent
steps: Remove the bowl from the heat and let the mixture cool slightly — fragrance added to hot oil simply evaporates away.
Stir in the 10 drops of orange essential oil and 5 drops of vanilla essential oil and mix well until the warm, creamsicle-like scent is even throughout.

sections.title: Jar, Set, and Finish
steps: Pour the scented mixture into the clean, sanitized jar or container.
Let the body butter cool and set undisturbed at room temperature until it firms to a soft, scoopable solid.
Cap the jar once fully set and label it with the ingredients and the date made.

tips: This butter is 100% oils with no water phase, so it needs no preservative — but always scoop with clean, dry fingers or a small spatula, because introduced water invites microbial growth.
An optional 0.5% of vitamin E stirred in at cool-down delays rancidity and extends the life of the sweet almond oil.
If your room runs warm, set the jar in the refrigerator to firm up; slow-cooled cocoa butter can otherwise set slightly grainy.
A little goes a long way — melt a pea-sized amount between your palms and press into damp skin after a shower.

orange-vanilla-dream-body-butter.cure_and_storage: Store the jar below about 75°F in a cool, dark place so the butter does not melt and lose its texture; kept dry and clean it lasts roughly 6-12 months, limited by the freshness of the oils. Discard it at any rancid, crayon-like odor or color change. No refrigeration is needed unless your home runs hot.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Spray your mixing bowl, spatula, and storage jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air-dry; a scrub is only as clean as the dirtiest tool that touched it.
Put on nitrile gloves so skin flora never enters the product.
Measure the 1 cup of brown sugar, 1/4 cup of cashew nut oil, 1/4 cup of finely chopped cashews, and 1 tablespoon of honey.

sections.title: Mix the Scrub Base
steps: In the mixing bowl, combine the brown sugar and cashew nut oil, folding with the spatula until every sugar crystal is evenly coated.
Check the texture: it should resemble wet sand that loosely holds together when squeezed — add a spoonful more sugar if soupy, or a drizzle more cashew oil if dusty.

sections.title: Add the Cashews and Honey
steps: Add the finely chopped cashews for their extra polish and vitamin E, and the honey for its humectant draw, then mix thoroughly until uniform.
Chop the cashews truly fine — large pieces are too sharp for skin and sink to the jar's bottom.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Spoon the scrub into the clean jar, pressing gently to remove air pockets, then wipe the rim and seal immediately.
Label the jar with the ingredients and a use-by date, and note that it is a body scrub rather than a face scrub.
Include a small dry scoop with the jar so no one dips wet fingers into it.

tips: Brown sugar is the gentlest of the sugar exfoliants, and paired with soft cashew pieces this scrub suits even delicate skin areas.
This scrub contains no preservative, so keeping shower water out of the jar is everything — decant a single use into a small dish before you step in.
Because it is a nut-based product, label it clearly: anyone with a tree-nut allergy should not use it.
Oily scrubs make the tub slippery — rinse the floor after use.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.
cashew-cream-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store the sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place away from shower steam; unpreserved and kept perfectly dry it deserves a conservative 3-month use-by date, and never longer than the best-by date of the cashew nut oil. Scoop only with dry hands or a spoon, and discard immediately at any off smell, color change, or pooled water in the jar.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Spray your mixing bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air-dry, and put on nitrile gloves before touching any ingredient.
Measure the 1 cup of brown sugar, 1/4 cup of coconut oil, 10 drops of frankincense essential oil, and the optional 1 tablespoon of dried frankincense resin.
If your coconut oil is solid, warm it just until soft — pouring hot oil over sugar melts it into syrup.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: In the mixing bowl, combine the brown sugar and coconut oil, folding until every crystal is coated and the texture resembles wet sand that holds together loosely when squeezed.
Adjust if needed: a spoonful more brown sugar if it looks oily, a little more coconut oil if it is dusty and crumbly.

sections.title: Add the Frankincense
steps: Add the 10 drops of frankincense essential oil and mix thoroughly so the woody, earthy aroma is even throughout.
If desired, stir in the tablespoon of dried frankincense resin for extra fragrance and a gentle textural crunch — crush any large tears first so they are not sharp on skin.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Spoon the scrub into the clean jar, pressing gently to remove air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal immediately.
Label the jar with the ingredients and a use-by date, and note the slip hazard oily scrubs create on shower floors.
Keep a small dry spoon with the jar so wet fingers never dip into the product.

tips: Brown sugar is the softest exfoliant, and with frankincense's calming aroma this works as a wind-down evening scrub.
Resin pieces do not dissolve in the shower — keep them small or leave them out if you dislike the texture.
A 4 oz jar beats one big jar: it gets used up before water or rancidity can win.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
frankincense-fusion-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store sealed in a cool, dark, dry place away from shower steam; unpreserved but kept perfectly dry it carries a conservative 3-month use-by date, never beyond the coconut oil's own best-by. Scoop with dry hands only and discard at any off smell, mold, or pooled water in the jar.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, let them air-dry, and put on gloves.
Measure the 1 cup of white sugar, 1/4 cup of almond oil, 10 drops of sandalwood essential oil, and the optional 1 tablespoon of dried sandalwood powder.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the white sugar and almond oil in the bowl, folding until every crystal is evenly coated in a wet-sand texture.
Fine-tune with a spoonful more sugar or a drizzle more almond oil until the scrub loosely holds together when squeezed.

sections.title: Add the Sandalwood
steps: Add the 10 drops of sandalwood essential oil and mix thoroughly for the calming, grounding scent.
If desired, sift in the tablespoon of dried sandalwood powder for extra fragrance and its skin-soothing effect, stirring until no dry pockets remain.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Spoon the scrub into the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients and a use-by date, and add the standard slippery-tub caution.
Store a dry scoop with the jar so the product stays water-free.
To use, massage a small handful over damp skin in gentle circles, letting the white sugar polish while the almond oil conditions, then rinse warm and pat dry.

tips: White sugar is the all-purpose workhorse grit — gentler than salt, firmer than brown sugar.
Sandalwood powder can shadow the scrub slightly tan; mix well so the color is even rather than streaky.
Almond oil rinses lighter than coconut, leaving a satin rather than greasy finish.

Never use crushed walnut shell (or other crushed nut shells) in a facial scrub — the shells fracture into jagged, serrated-edged shards that can cause micro-tears in skin. For the face choose round, smooth particles instead: spherical jojoba beads or fine sugar, which have rounded edges and dissolve or deform under pressure.

Emulsified scrubs (made with emulsifying wax) turn into a lotion-like layer and rinse clean with water; plain oil-and-sugar scrubs leave an oil film behind. Either way, always warn users that oil-based scrubs make the tub or shower floor dangerously slippery both during use and until the residue is cleaned off.

Any scrub used in the shower or dipped into with wet hands will get water in the jar, so it needs a broad-spectrum preservative: liquid Germall Plus at 0.1-0.5% (0.5% is the standard choice for scrubs) or Optiphen at 0.75-1.5% of total weight. Note Optiphen Plus is water-soluble and hard to incorporate into anhydrous scrubs — for purely oil-based formulas an oil-soluble preservative like Phenonip is the better fit.

Scrubs containing fresh, non-dehydrated ingredients (citrus peel or zest, fresh herbs, used coffee grounds) last only about 1-2 weeks even refrigerated — make small batches and store them in the fridge. By contrast, a plain sugar- or salt-plus-oil scrub keeps for months at room temperature and longer refrigerated, provided no water or wet fingers contaminate the jar.
sandalwood-soothe-scrub.cure_and_storage: Keep the sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry spot away from bathroom steam; dry and unpreserved it merits a 3-month use-by date bounded by the almond oil's freshness. Use dry hands or a spoon and discard at any off smell or moisture in the jar.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, air-dry, and glove up.
Measure the 1 cup of sea salt, 1/4 cup of jojoba oil, 10 drops of juniper berry essential oil, and the optional 1 tablespoon of dried juniper berries.

sections.title: Mix the Salt and Oil Base
steps: Combine the sea salt and jojoba oil in the bowl, folding until every grain is coated and the mix holds together like damp sand.
Remember salt is the aggressive exfoliant choice — suited to rough spots, elbows, and feet rather than delicate areas.

sections.title: Add the Juniper
steps: Add the 10 drops of juniper berry essential oil and mix thoroughly for the fresh, gin-like lift.
If desired, stir in the dried juniper berries, lightly crushed, for fragrance, texture, and a scatter of deep blue color.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Pack the scrub into the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients and a use-by date, plus two warnings the salt demands: not for freshly shaved, broken, or irritated skin, and mind the slippery tub.
Include a dry scoop so no wet fingers enter the jar.
To use, work a scoop over damp feet, elbows, and rough patches in firm circles, letting the sea salt buff while the jojoba oil conditions, then rinse thoroughly.

tips: Salt stings on freshly shaved or broken skin — schedule this scrub for before, not after, shaving.
Jojoba is technically a liquid wax that resists rancidity, giving this scrub a longer natural life than most.
Fine sea salt polishes; coarse sea salt on soft skin scratches — match the grain to the body part.

Formulate salt bars with 50-100% of the oil weight in fine-grain sea salt (beginners start at 50%) and a coconut-oil-heavy base with a high superfat, because salt suppresses lather; Soap Queen's salt bar runs 50% coconut oil and many formulas go 80-100% coconut with 15-20% superfat.

Cut salt bars EARLY, in hours not days: salt makes the batter harden extremely fast, so a loaf must be unmolded and cut as soon as it is firm, roughly 1-6 hours after pouring depending on the recipe. Wait overnight and the loaf crumbles when cut. Individual cavity molds sidestep the timing problem entirely.

Use plain fine sea salt or Himalayan pink salt, not Dead Sea salt or Epsom salt. Dead Sea salt's very high mineral content is strongly hygroscopic, pulling moisture from the air and producing weepy, sweaty, soft bars.

Add fruit or vegetable purees at thin trace. Sugary purees (strawberry, banana, mango) speed up trace and heat the soap, so soap at cooler temperatures, skip insulation, and refrigerate or freeze the mold after pouring, since overheated sugar can crack, volcano, or caramelize the bar to a dull brown.
juniper-joy-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store sealed in a cool, dark, dry place; the salt base plus stable jojoba keeps well, but water is still the enemy, so keep shower spray out and use within about 3 months unpreserved. Salt slowly dissolves into any moisture, so a watery layer in the jar means it is time to discard.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, air-dry, and put on gloves.
Measure the 1 cup of brown sugar, 1/4 cup of sweet almond oil, and 10 drops of neroli essential oil, and zest the orange if you are using the optional zest.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the brown sugar and sweet almond oil, folding until the mixture is a uniform, wet-sand consistency.
Adjust with more sugar or a drizzle more oil until it squeezes into a loose clump.

sections.title: Add the Neroli and Zest
steps: Add the 10 drops of neroli essential oil and mix thoroughly for the calming orange-blossom scent.
If desired, fold in the zest of one orange for a brighter citrus note and flecks of color — pat the zest dry first so it adds no moisture.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Spoon the scrub into the clean jar, press gently to remove air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients and a use-by date, and note that fresh zest shortens the product's life.
Keep a dry scoop with the jar.
To use, smooth a scoop over damp skin in slow circles, letting the brown sugar melt as the sweet almond oil and neroli sink in, then rinse warm.

tips: Neroli is precious — 10 drops perfumes the whole cup of sugar, so resist adding more.
Fresh orange zest carries a little water: if you include it, treat the scrub as short-dated and store it extra carefully, or refrigerate.
Brown sugar plus almond oil makes this soft enough for decolletage and arms, not just feet.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
neroli-nectar-scrub.cure_and_storage: Without the zest, store sealed, cool, dark, and dry with a 3-month use-by date; with fresh zest folded in, refrigerate and use within 2-3 weeks. Either way scoop only with dry hands and discard at any off smell, mold, or pooled moisture.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, air-dry, and glove up.
Measure the 1 cup of granulated sugar, 1/4 cup of almond oil, and 10 drops of geranium essential oil, and gather the optional fresh geranium petals.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the granulated sugar and almond oil in the bowl until well mixed and every crystal is coated — the recipe's own recovered steps call for exactly this simple fold.
Check for the wet-sand squeeze test and adjust sugar or oil a spoonful at a time.

sections.title: Add the Geranium
steps: Add the 10 drops of geranium essential oil and mix thoroughly for the rosy, balancing floral scent.
If desired, fold in the fresh geranium petals for fragrance and botanical beauty, knowing fresh plant material makes the jar perishable.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Spoon the scrub into the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients and a use-by date reflecting whether petals went in.
Include a dry scoop and keep the jar away from direct shower spray.
To use, polish damp skin in gentle circles with a scoop of the geranium-scented sugar, then rinse warm and pat dry.

tips: Geranium essential oil is a rose-like scent at a fraction of rose's price — this scrub smells far more luxurious than its ingredient list.
Fresh petals are lovely for a same-week gift jar but shorten shelf life dramatically; use dried petals for a longer-lived batch.
Granulated sugar gives a medium polish suitable for all-over body use.

Lavender is the workhorse floral essential oil: it survives saponification well and The Nerdy Farm Wife's chart works with about 23 g (0.8 oz) of lavender essential oil per pound (454 g) of oils, one of the more generous floral rates.

For ylang ylang, use grade II or III in soap. The premium grades (Super Extra, Extra, I) are reserved for perfumery because their allergen levels force very low usage rates; ylang ylang II/III can be used at up to 3%, about 0.48 oz (13.6 g) per pound of oils.

Dried lavender buds and rose petals turn brown wherever they touch the alkaline soap batter; calendula is the notable exception that stays golden. To decorate with buds anyway, unmold after 24-48 hours, mist the tops with rubbing alcohol, sprinkle the buds on, and mist again so they stick. The color then holds for weeks to months instead of browning immediately.

Floral fragrance oils (rose and jasmine types especially) are prone to accelerating trace. Work at light trace with slow-moving liquid oils such as olive or sweet almond, soap on the cooler side, add the fragrance last, and stir it in by hand with a whisk rather than stick-blending.
geranium-garden-scrub.cure_and_storage: Petal-free, the sealed jar keeps about 3 months in a cool, dark, dry place limited by the almond oil's date; with fresh geranium petals folded in, refrigerate and finish it within 1-2 weeks. Discard at the first sign of moisture, mold, or an off smell.

Soften solid coconut oil just to workable — never hot — so the sugar does not dissolve.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the white sugar and coconut oil until well mixed, with every crystal coated and the texture like wet sand.
Adjust to a loose squeeze-clump with an extra spoonful of sugar or drizzle of oil as needed.

sections.title: Add the Tea Tree
steps: Add the 10 drops of tea tree essential oil and mix thoroughly — its antimicrobial, clarifying character is the point of this scrub.
If desired, add the dried tea tree leaves for extra fragrance and texture, as the recipe's recovered steps describe.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Transfer the scrub to the clean jar, pressing out air pockets, then wipe the rim and seal.
Label with ingredients, a use-by date, and a body-use note — tea tree at scrub strength is for backs, shoulders, and feet more than faces.
Keep a dry scoop with the jar.

tips: This is the scrub for blemish-prone backs and shoulders — the tea tree targets the same bacteria involved in body breakouts.
Tea tree's own antimicrobial nature helps the jar resist contamination, but it is not a substitute for keeping water out.
Coconut oil firms up in a cold bathroom; let the jar warm a minute before scooping.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
tea-tree-tingle-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store sealed in a cool, dark, dry spot with a conservative 3-month use-by date unpreserved, never past the coconut oil's best-by. Scoop dry, keep shower spray out, and discard at any off smell or pooled water.

tips: Olive oil leaves a noticeable moisture film — wonderful for dry winter skin, heavier than almond or grapeseed for summer.

Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
sage-sanctuary-scrub.cure_and_storage: Leaf-free, store sealed in a cool, dark, dry place for up to 3 months, bounded by the olive oil's freshness; with fresh sage folded in, refrigerate and use within 1-2 weeks. Discard at any off or rancid smell, mold, or moisture in the jar.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, air-dry, and glove up — doubly important in a scrub containing fresh fruit.
Measure the 1 cup of white sugar and 1/4 cup of coconut oil, mash the 1/4 cup of watermelon, and zest the lime as the recipe's recovered steps list.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the white sugar and coconut oil until well mixed into a coated, wet-sand texture.
Work quickly from here — the fruit will begin dissolving the sugar the moment it goes in.

sections.title: Add the Watermelon and Lime
steps: Add the mashed watermelon and lime zest, then mix thoroughly; the fruit brings vitamins A, B, and C and turns the scrub a fresh pink.
Expect a softer, wetter texture than a standard sugar scrub — that is the watermelon's high water content.

sections.title: Jar, Label, and Chill
steps: Transfer the scrub to the clean jar, wipe the rim, and seal immediately.
Label it clearly as a fresh, refrigerated product with a made-on date.
Refrigerate at once — fresh watermelon makes this a perishable cosmetic, not a shelf product.
To use within its short life, massage the chilled pink scrub over damp skin, let the watermelon juices refresh for a minute, then rinse cool.

tips: This is really a fresh treatment, not a pantry scrub: make small batches and think of it like a smoothie for your skin.
An unpreserved water-containing scrub can grow mold and bacteria within days at room temperature — the fridge is non-negotiable.
Use it as a single-session shower scrub party: mix, use generously, share, and discard leftovers without guilt.

Never use crushed walnut shell (or other crushed nut shells) in a facial scrub — the shells fracture into jagged, serrated-edged shards that can cause micro-tears in skin. For the face choose round, smooth particles instead: spherical jojoba beads or fine sugar, which have rounded edges and dissolve or deform under pressure.

Emulsified scrubs (made with emulsifying wax) turn into a lotion-like layer and rinse clean with water; plain oil-and-sugar scrubs leave an oil film behind. Either way, always warn users that oil-based scrubs make the tub or shower floor dangerously slippery both during use and until the residue is cleaned off.

Any scrub used in the shower or dipped into with wet hands will get water in the jar, so it needs a broad-spectrum preservative: liquid Germall Plus at 0.1-0.5% (0.5% is the standard choice for scrubs) or Optiphen at 0.75-1.5% of total weight. Note Optiphen Plus is water-soluble and hard to incorporate into anhydrous scrubs — for purely oil-based formulas an oil-soluble preservative like Phenonip is the better fit.

Scrubs containing fresh, non-dehydrated ingredients (citrus peel or zest, fresh herbs, used coffee grounds) last only about 1-2 weeks even refrigerated — make small batches and store them in the fridge. By contrast, a plain sugar- or salt-plus-oil scrub keeps for months at room temperature and longer refrigerated, provided no water or wet fingers contaminate the jar.
watermelon-wave-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store only in the refrigerator and use within 3-5 days, scooping with a clean dry spoon each time; freeze single portions if you want it to last longer. At any off smell, fizzing, mold, or separation, discard the jar — fresh fruit plus sugar is a perfect microbial growth medium.
