Measure the 1 cup of granulated sugar, 1/4 cup of khorasan oil, and 1/4 cup of finely ground khorasan flakes, and zest the lemon.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the granulated sugar and khorasan oil until well mixed into an evenly coated base.

sections.title: Add the Khorasan Flakes and Lemon
steps: Add the finely ground khorasan flakes and lemon zest, then mix thoroughly; the antioxidant-rich ancient-wheat meal softens the scrub while the zest brightens it.
Grind the flakes evenly so the polish stays calm and scratch-free, true to the name.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Transfer the scrub to the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients, a use-by date shortened for the fresh zest, and a wheat/gluten note.
Keep a dry scoop with the jar.
To use, buff damp skin in calm, light circles with the buttery grain polish, then rinse warm.
Stir before each use so the ground flakes and zest stay evenly mixed.

tips: Khorasan is the same ancient wheat sold as Kamut — buttery-scented and gentle when finely ground.
Ground flakes act like colloidal oats, calming as much as polishing.
Dry the lemon zest thoroughly; it is the only moisture risk in an otherwise shelf-friendly formula.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
khorasan-kalm-scrub.cure_and_storage: With fresh lemon zest, refrigerate and use within 2-3 weeks; a zest-free batch keeps about 3 months sealed in a cool, dark, dry spot, bounded by the khorasan oil's date. Scoop dry and discard at any off smell or moisture.

sections.title: Sanitize and Prepare
steps: Sanitize the bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol, air-dry, and put on gloves.
Measure the 1 cup of white sugar, 1/4 cup of farro oil, and 1/4 cup of farro grains, and zest the lime listed in the recipe's recovered detail.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the white sugar and farro oil until well mixed, per the recipe's own steps.

sections.title: Add the Farro and Lime
steps: Add the farro grains, cracked or coarsely ground, and the lime zest, then mix thoroughly; the antioxidant-rich grain adds hearty polish under the bright lime.
Crack the farro first — whole dry farro berries are too hard for skin.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Transfer the scrub to the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients, a use-by date shortened for the fresh lime zest, and a wheat/gluten note.
Keep a dry scoop with the jar.
To use, scrub damp heels, knees, and elbows in firm circles with the cracked-grain polish, then rinse thoroughly.
Stir before use so the heavier grain meal lifts back through the sugar.

tips: Pulse the farro in a spice grinder to a coarse meal — that is the difference between polish and scratch.
Lime zest fades fast; make small batches so the scent is always fresh.
White sugar plus cracked farro suits rough zones like heels, knees, and elbows especially well.

Never use crushed walnut shell (or other crushed nut shells) in a facial scrub — the shells fracture into jagged, serrated-edged shards that can cause micro-tears in skin. For the face choose round, smooth particles instead: spherical jojoba beads or fine sugar, which have rounded edges and dissolve or deform under pressure.

Emulsified scrubs (made with emulsifying wax) turn into a lotion-like layer and rinse clean with water; plain oil-and-sugar scrubs leave an oil film behind. Either way, always warn users that oil-based scrubs make the tub or shower floor dangerously slippery both during use and until the residue is cleaned off.

Any scrub used in the shower or dipped into with wet hands will get water in the jar, so it needs a broad-spectrum preservative: liquid Germall Plus at 0.1-0.5% (0.5% is the standard choice for scrubs) or Optiphen at 0.75-1.5% of total weight. Note Optiphen Plus is water-soluble and hard to incorporate into anhydrous scrubs — for purely oil-based formulas an oil-soluble preservative like Phenonip is the better fit.

Scrubs containing fresh, non-dehydrated ingredients (citrus peel or zest, fresh herbs, used coffee grounds) last only about 1-2 weeks even refrigerated — make small batches and store them in the fridge. By contrast, a plain sugar- or salt-plus-oil scrub keeps for months at room temperature and longer refrigerated, provided no water or wet fingers contaminate the jar.
farro-fantasy-scrub.cure_and_storage: With fresh lime zest, refrigerate and use within 2-3 weeks; zest-free it keeps about 3 months sealed, cool, dark, and dry, limited by the farro oil's date. Scoop dry and discard at any off smell or dampness.

sections.title: Mix the Sugar and Oil Base
steps: Combine the granulated sugar and barley oil until well mixed into an evenly coated base.

sections.title: Add the Barley Flakes and Peppermint
steps: Add the finely ground barley flakes and the teaspoon of peppermint essential oil, then mix thoroughly; the soft flake meal polishes while the mint delivers the cooling breeze of the name.
Hold to the stated teaspoon of peppermint and keep the finished scrub away from the face and freshly shaved skin.

sections.title: Jar and Label
steps: Transfer the scrub to the clean jar, press out air pockets, wipe the rim, and seal.
Label with ingredients, a use-by date, a body-only note for the mint, and a gluten note.
Keep a dry scoop with the jar and store it away from shower spray.
To use, massage the cool minty polish over damp skin in brisk circles, letting the barley meal buffer the sugar, then rinse.
Save it for morning showers — the peppermint chill is a natural wake-up.

tips: This is Barley Bliss's morning twin: same gentle grain base, peppermint instead of lavender.
The cooling mint feels strongest in a warm shower — a natural summer scrub.
Ground barley flakes behave like oatmeal, buffering the sugar for sensitive skin.

Lovely Greens caps peppermint essential oil at 2% of the recipe by weight, about 0.32 oz (9 g, roughly 2 tsp) per pound (454 g) of oils. Its menthol genuinely triggers cold receptors in the skin, so the lather feels cooling: keep peppermint bars away from eyes and sensitive areas, and go easy on the rate for face or kids' soap. Spearmint's limit is far lower, 0.25%, because of its carvone content.

Eucalyptus, tea tree, and rosemary essential oils can each be used at up to about 3% (0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils). When blending several herbal oils in one bar, calculate each oil's share so the combined total stays within the limits.

Skip sage essential oil in soap. The Nerdy Farm Wife excludes it from her soapmaking chart because of its many safety warnings and contraindications; clary sage (usable around 3%, 13 g per pound of oils) or a rosemary-herbal blend gives a similar note safely.

Add dried herbs fully dried and finely pulsed; the mint from a plain tea bag works perfectly. The specks decorate rather than scent the bar, and over time each fleck develops a small golden halo as its tea seeps into the surrounding soap, a signature look of herbal tea soaps.
barley-breeze-scrub.cure_and_storage: Store sealed in a cool, dark, dry place with a conservative 3-month use-by date bounded by the barley oil's freshness; scoop with dry hands, keep water out of the jar, and discard at any off smell or moisture.

sections.title: Set up and mix the dry base
steps: Put on gloves, a dust mask, and safety glasses, and work in a well-ventilated, low-humidity room - ambient moisture is the number one cause of failed bath bombs, and fine citric acid dust is irritating to skin and lungs.
In a large non-reactive mixing bowl, combine the 1 cup baking soda, 1/2 cup citric acid, 1/2 cup Epsom salt, and 1/2 cup cornstarch.
Sift the baking soda and citric acid or break up every clump with gloved fingers, then whisk the dry mix for a full minute so the citric acid is evenly distributed.

sections.title: Add the lavender wet ingredients
steps: In a small container, stir together the 2 tablespoons almond oil and 10-15 drops lavender essential oil.
Drizzle the oil mixture slowly into the dry ingredients while whisking constantly, then rub the mixture between gloved fingers to break up any oily pockets.
Stir in the 1 tablespoon dried lavender buds and keep mixing until the buds are evenly scattered and the mixture resembles wet sand with no streaks.

sections.title: Reach packing consistency and mold
steps: Do the squeeze test: grab a handful and squeeze hard - it should clump like damp sand; if it crumbles, spritz 2-3 pumps of witch hazel over the surface while mixing, and repeat in small rounds until it just holds together.
Overfill both halves of your bath bomb mold, pressing lightly to compact the bottom of each half while leaving the top surface loose.
Press the two halves together firmly in one straight motion without twisting - twisting shears the seam and the bomb will split later.
Wipe away the ring of excess mixture at the seam, tap the mold gently, lift off the top half, and let the bomb rest in the bottom half about 15 minutes before releasing it.

sections.title: Dry and finish
steps: Set the finished bombs on a parchment-lined tray or folded towel and let them dry for 24 hours in a cool, dry room away from bathrooms and direct fan airflow, as the recipe directs.
Check that each bomb feels rock-hard before handling; in humid weather give them up to 48 hours or briefly refrigerate them to firm up.
Once dry, remove any bombs still in molds and store them in an airtight container so they stop absorbing atmospheric moisture.

tips: Press a small pinch of the dried lavender buds into one mold half before packing so the flowers show on the face of the finished bomb.
Because this recipe carries 2 tablespoons of almond oil, consider adding polysorbate 80 at about one-third the oil weight so the oil disperses in the bathwater instead of making the tub slippery.
Make these on a dry day if you can - a rainy, humid day measurably increases warting and cracking.

To color the water without a tub ring, pair micas or lake dyes with polysorbate 80 — an emulsifier that carries pigment and carrier oils into the bath water instead of letting them pool on top or cling to the tub. Dose poly 80 relative to your oils (commonly about 50-100% of the oil weight). Lakes disperse and tint the water; micas mainly add sparkle and will sink or streak the tub without an emulsifier.

Scent bath bombs at roughly 2-3% fragrance by weight of the dry mix (about 1 teaspoon / 5 ml per pound) for good scent retention, and always confirm the fragrance's own bath-product safe usage cap. Vanillin-containing fragrances discolor bombs too — often weeks or months later — so use clear, vanilla-free fragrances for white or pastel designs.

For layered and embed designs, keep the whole batch at an even 'wet sand' consistency built on the standard 2:1 baking soda to citric acid base: a too-dry mix makes layers crumble apart at the seams, while a too-wet mix starts fizzing prematurely and expands or cracks the bomb in the mold. Pack each layer firmly before adding the next.

Polysorbate 80 alone produces very little foam — for a foaming bath bomb add SLSA (sodium lauryl sulfoacetate), a mild powdered surfactant that creates real suds on top of the fizz. Wear a dust mask when handling SLSA powder.
lavender-fields-bliss-bath-bomb.cure_and_storage: Air-dry 24 hours (up to 48 in humidity) until rock-hard, then keep in an airtight container or shrink wrap in a cool, dry, dark place - never a bathroom cabinet. Use within about 6 months for maximum fizz.

sections.title: Plan the dilution and gather supplies
steps: Set out a clean 1 fl oz (30 mL) glass bottle - amber or cobalt glass protects the oils from light.

This blend follows the safe topical guideline of roughly 1% dilution: 6 drops of essential oil total in 1 fl oz (30 mL) of jojoba oil, which is the gentle level recommended for daily emotional-support massage.
Have the recipe's oils ready: 3 drops Roman Chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile), 2 drops Lavender (Lavandula angustifolia), and 1 drop Sweet Orange (Citrus sinensis).

sections.title: Blend the oils
steps: Pour the 1 fl oz (30 mL) of jojoba oil into the bottle.
Add the 3 drops Roman chamomile, 2 drops lavender, and 1 drop sweet orange directly to the jojoba, counting drops carefully.
Cap the bottle and shake gently until the oils are fully blended, as the published directions instruct.

The recipe's richer conifer variation uses 9 drops 4 Conifer Blend, 4 drops lavender, 3 drops frankincense, and 2 drops sweet orange in a separate 1 fl oz of jojoba - make it the same way in its own labeled bottle if you want the forest-forward version.

sections.title: Use and safety
steps: Massage a small amount into the chest, back, or feet at bedtime, per the published directions.
Patch test on the inner forearm and wait 24 hours before regular use; discontinue if redness or itching appears.
Do not use on children under two, and check with a doctor before use in pregnancy; keep the bottle capped and out of children's reach.
Aromatherapy supports mood but is not a treatment for clinical depression - seek professional help for persistent low mood.

tips: Roman chamomile and lavender are among the gentlest calming oils, which is why this blend suits nightly use.
Jojoba is technically a liquid wax and resists rancidity, giving this blend a long shelf life.
Label the bottle with the contents, dilution, and date so bedtime use stays consistent.

Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.

Set the cup in a saucepan with a few centimeters of barely simmering water (or use a tea warmer, as the published directions suggest) and melt the beeswax gently - never over direct heat.

sections.title: Combine oil and wax
steps: Once the beeswax is melted, add the jojoba oil to the cup.
If the wax starts to re-solidify when the cooler oil goes in, return the cup to the water bath and re-melt gently, then remove from heat.
Let the mixture cool for a minute off the heat so the essential oils are not flashed off by the hot wax.

steps: Stir in the recipe's respiratory blend: 8 drops 4 Conifer Blend, 5 drops Eucalyptus radiata, and 2 drops Lavender (Lavandula angustifolia).
Pour the liquid rub into the 2 oz tin or glass jar and put the lid on once a skin forms.
Allow the rub to cool and set fully - undisturbed at room temperature - before first use.

sections.title: Prepare the diffuser
steps: Set out your ultrasonic diffuser and the three oils the recipe calls for: lemon, tea tree, and lavender.
Fill the diffuser with clean water to its fill line - most home units hold 100-300 mL.
Place the diffuser on a stable surface in a ventilated room, away from the edge of shelves and out of children's reach.

sections.title: Add the blend
steps: Add the 3 drops lemon essential oil (Citrus limon), 3 drops tea tree essential oil (Melaleuca alternifolia), and 3 drops lavender essential oil (Lavandula angustifolia) to the water, per the recipe.
If kids or pets share the space, halve the drops as the recipe directs, keep the door open so animals can leave, and be especially cautious with cats and caged birds.
As the recipe's alternative, you can instead add 3 drops of each oil to the wick of a personal inhaler for an on-the-go version.

sections.title: Run and maintain
steps: Run the diffuser intermittently - 30-60 minutes on, then 30-60 minutes off; intermittent diffusion is both safer and more effective because the nervous system habituates after about an hour.
Stop diffusing if anyone develops a headache or nausea, and shorten sessions around pregnant women or infants.
Reach for this light, refreshing blend to freshen a stale room, clear cooking odors, or lift the mood in a workspace.
Empty and wipe the reservoir between blends so old oils do not build up, and deep-clean the unit monthly per its manual.

sections.title: Understand the blend
steps: This is a master essential-oil blend built from conifer oils, including Balsam Fir (Abies balsamea) with beta-pinene and delta-3-carene for a decongestant, opening quality, Sitka Spruce (Picea sitchensis) with beta-myrcene and piperitone for a mucolytic, cleansing action, and White Spruce (Picea glauca) with camphor and bornyl acetate for a clarifying, steadying character.

The blend is designed to support clear breathing, steady the mind and nervous system, and gently purify the air - and, importantly, it is the conifer alternative used because eucalyptus and ravintsara are avoided in children's recipes.

Combine equal parts of the conifer oils in a small amber bottle, cap, and roll gently to mix; label it 4 Conifer Blend so other recipes in this collection (chest rub, kids massage oil, bedtime blend) can draw from it.

sections.title: Use at the published rates
steps: Topical: dilute 5 to 6 drops per 1 oz of carrier oil for kids, or 15 to 18 drops per 1 oz for adults, following the recipe's own dilution table.

Diffuser: use 5 to 6 drops per run for everyone - the recipe uses the same diffuser dose for kids as adults, with proper ventilation.
Never apply the undiluted blend directly to skin.

sections.title: Safety
steps: Diffuse in ventilated rooms with the door open, especially around children and pets, and run the diffuser intermittently rather than continuously.
Patch test any topical dilution on the inner forearm and wait 24 hours before wider use.
Keep the master bottle capped, labeled, and locked away from children.
Conifer oils oxidize with age - replace the blend if it smells flat or turpentine-sharp rather than fresh and green.

tips: Mixing the master blend once and dosing from it keeps every chest rub, inhaler, and diffuser session at a consistent ratio.

Store conifer oils in the refrigerator to slow oxidation if you make a large master bottle.

Patchouli and cedarwood are true base notes that survive saponification and the cure far better than citrus or floral tops — build wood blends around them as the anchor. Lovely Greens' safety-assessed maximum for both is 3% of the recipe by weight (about 0.48 oz / 13.6 g per pound of oils).

Patchouli genuinely improves with age: its main constituent patchoulol slowly oxidizes, so the oil — and soap scented with it — deepens and mellows over months. Buy or set aside aged patchouli when you can, and store the oil in amber glass, cool and dark, to steer that aging in the right direction.

Sandalwood powder is best treated as a natural tan-to-reddish colorant additive in cold process soap, not as a reliable scent source.

sections.title: Combine and cool slightly

steps: Set out a food processor, a glass or ceramic bowl, and a non-metal stirrer - avoid metal bowls and spoons because wet clay can pick up metal ions and lose effectiveness.

sections.title: Set up safely and prepare the humectant base
steps: This is a syndet (synthetic-detergent) bar - no lye and pH-balanced for hair - and the recipe makes 200 grams of product, or two 3-ounce bars; weigh everything on a scale that reads to 0.1 g.

Before opening any surfactant container, put on your respirator or fine-particle dust mask, safety glasses, and gloves, and work in a well-ventilated area - airborne SCI powder is very irritating to the lungs.
Measure the 1 gram cationic guar gum and 10 grams glycerin and mix together until the guar gum is fully dispersed - this slurry step prevents clumps later.

Measure the 14 grams argan oil, 6 grams castor oil, and 4 grams D-panthenol powder, add them to the guar-glycerin mixture, and stir well; the panthenol may take time to dissolve, so mix and let it sit briefly until no clumps remain.

sections.title: Add preservative, antioxidant, and fragrance
steps: Measure the 2 grams Optiphen preservative, 1 gram vitamin E oil, and 2 grams essential or fragrance oils (optional) and stir them into the mixture - the preservative is required because the bar lives in a wet shower.

If blending your own scent, the booklet suggests combos like Fresh and Clean Scalp (50% lavender, 25% tea tree, 25% peppermint) or Bright and Uplifting (50% lemongrass, 25% sweet orange, 25% grapefruit), pre-mixed in a separate bottle; verify custom blends at EOCALC.com using Category 9 (wash-off products) for a 200 g batch.

sections.title: Add the liquid surfactant and clay
steps: Add the 40 grams cocamidopropyl betaine and 5 grams kaolin clay to the mixture and mix until combined.
The betaine boosts foam and supplies the moisture that lets the bars mold instead of crumbling, while the kaolin absorbs excess scalp oil and gives the bar a silky feel.

sections.title: Incorporate the SCI and knead the dough
steps: Double-check that your respirator, safety glasses, and gloves are still on and ventilation is good - this is the dustiest step.
Measure the 120 grams sodium cocoyl isethionate (SCI) powder and add it to the mixture.
Start mixing with a utensil; when the mass thickens into a dough, switch to kneading with gloved hands until fully combined and uniform, with no dry powder pockets.

sections.title: Shape, cure, and store
steps: Form the dough by hand into two pucks or press it firmly into a mold; if using a bar press, line it with plastic wrap for easy removal.
Let the bars harden for 24 hours before first use, per the recipe.
To use, swipe the bar over wet hair a few times or lather in hands, massage into the scalp, and rinse - no vinegar rinse needed since the bar is pH-balanced.
Store finished bars in a cool, dry place and use within 1 year; between showers keep the bar on a draining dish out of the water stream.

tips: SCI is nicknamed baby foam for its mildness, and pairing it with cocamidopropyl betaine mellows the cleanse further while making the dough workable.
If the dough stiffens before you finish shaping, brief gentle warmth (a minute over a water bath) re-softens it.
For sale or gifting, label with INCI names in descending order - the booklet lists the full INCI declaration - plus net weight and your business details.
shampoo-bar.cure_and_storage: Harden 24 hours before use. Store spares cool, dry, and dark for up to 1 year; the bar in use lasts longest on a draining rack or soap dish where it dries fully between showers.

sections.title: Weigh and melt the base
steps: This BTMS-50 conditioner bar is lye-free and makes 200 grams of product - about two 3-ounce bars; sanitize your molds and tools and weigh every ingredient on a 0.1 g scale.
Weigh the 40 grams murumuru butter, 26 grams unrefined argan oil, 70 grams BTMS-50 emulsifying wax, 36 grams cetyl alcohol, and 6 grams stearic acid into a heat-safe bowl.
Place the bowl over a double boiler and heat gently until fully melted - BTMS-50 pellets are the last to disappear; never melt over direct heat.

Note that BTMS-50 is the cationic conditioning heart of the formula - regular emulsifying wax looks similar but will not condition hair, so no substitutions there (the butter, by contrast, can swap for mango butter).

sections.title: Prepare the glycerin mixture
steps: In a separate bowl, combine the 14 grams glycerin, 4 grams cationic guar gum, and 4 grams panthenol powder.
Stir until smooth with no clumps - the panthenol may need to rest in the glycerin for a few minutes to fully dissolve.

sections.title: Pre-measure the cool-down ingredients
steps: In a small container, weigh out the 2 grams vitamin E oil, 2 grams Optiphen preservative, and 4 grams essential oils (optional), and set aside.
If scenting, the booklet's wash-off blends work here too (for example Natural Spa Day: 75% rosemary, 25% peppermint), verified at EOCALC.com under Category 9 for a 200 g batch.

sections.title: Combine at the right temperatures
steps: Once the base is fully melted, remove it from the heat and stir in the glycerin mixture until fully blended.
Allow the mixture to cool, stirring occasionally and checking the temperature with a thermometer.

When it drops below 140 F (60 C), stir in the pre-measured vitamin E, Optiphen, and essential oils - too hot and the preservative may burn off, too cool and the mixture solidifies before everything blends.

sections.title: Mold, set, and store
steps: Pour the mixture into molds and place them in the freezer for 4 hours - this lets the bars unmold without dents for a clean, professional finish.
Unmold by flexing the silicone gently once the bars are completely cold and hard.
To use, swipe the bar down the lengths and ends of clean, wet hair, work through with fingers or a wide comb, and rinse - focus on mid-lengths and ends, not the scalp.
Store away from sunlight and moisture, where bars last up to 1 year; once a bar starts touching water, use it within 3 months and let it dry on a draining dish between uses.

tips: The freezer set is not optional polish - a soft-unmolded bar dents and never looks right; give it the full 4 hours.
Murumuru butter seals in hydration and smooths frizz; mango butter is the recipe author's recommended substitute if you cannot source it.
Cetyl alcohol plus stearic acid is what keeps this bar hard in a warm shower - do not trim them to stretch other ingredients.
conditioner-bar.cure_and_storage: Freeze 4 hours to set, then store cured bars away from sunlight and moisture for up to 1 year; a bar in active shower use should be kept draining dry and used within 3 months.
